en: Preface to the *Vajra-śikya*: Emperor Yao could not do without Shun; King Wen could not do without Confucius. This is because the Way has that which it transmits.
Kāśyapa could not do without Kāśyapa (Kāśyapa Buddha); Kāśyapa Buddha could not do without Maitreya. This, too, is because the Way has that which it transmits.
Thus, that which was not seen in the Way during the time of Yao was heard of in the time of Shun; that which was not seen in the time of King Wen was heard of in the time of Confucius;
and that which was not awakened to in the time of Kāśyapa Muni was elucidated by Maitreya.
To posit a "Maitreya outside" [the Buddha] in order to clarify Kāśyapa Muni is like setting aside Confucius to investigate King Wen, or discarding Great Shun to examine Emperor Yao.
Is such a principle even possible? Moreover, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* expounded by Kāśyapa Muni is the most subtle and inconceivable;
even great sages who have ascended to the stages find it difficult to penetrate, yet they seek its illumination from Maitreya. How much more so for an ordinary person of the common world!

Why, then, do you reject their teachings and instead compose your own interpretations based on your personal views? Your language becomes ever more novel while the underlying meaning becomes ever more obscured;

your prose grows increasingly ornate while the essential intent becomes ever more darkened. Consequently, disputes arise in competition, and sectarian banners are raised in profusion. The corruption of the Dharma-ending age has reached its extreme.

Master Yunqi Zhuhong, however, has traveled far to exhaust the Great Canon and profoundly investigated the subtle words [of the sages]. He has repeatedly examined the various schools and comprehensively synthesized them.

I have consulted various scriptures and relied upon that foundational treatise to seek a comprehensive understanding of Maitreya’s verses. Furthermore, following Maitreya, I have used them to reach the sūtras of Kātyāyanīputra;

taking their underlying intent to explain the text and citing their words to corroborate my interpretations, I have sought not to make the language flowery, fearing it might obscure the principle, nor to make the expressions excessive, fearing it might weary the reader with prolixity, nor to make the topical divisions too fine, fearing they might interrupt the momentum of the prose.
Thus, it is hoped that those of future generations throughout the world will know that Maitreya’s verses are no different from Kāśyapa’s (Cāwen) sūtras;

and that the commentaries of Master K’ung are entirely derived from Maitreya’s verses. By means of the commentaries one comes to know the verses, and by means of the verses one comes to know the sūtras.
Then, those who were not clear regarding Kāśyapa’s teachings shall attain clarity through Maitreya, and those who attain clarity through Maitreya shall—
Thus, one who clearly understands Kāśyapa’s intent will not hold this interpretation; one who does not hold this interpretation is not a follower of Master K’ung (K’ung-shih).

One who grasps his intent will hold this interpretation; one who holds this interpretation is a follower of Maitreya. Alas! Throughout antiquity and the present, there have been no fewer than a thousand fascicles of commentaries on the *Vajracchedikā*.
Yet, only my Master Yunqi’s "Record of Feeling Like an Elephant" has truly captured the untransmitted teaching of Maitreya.

Master Kong was a true dragon and elephant of the Dharma-gate, having personally received the Master’s instructions to annotate this sutra. As various masters gathered like water flowing downward, opinions diverged across many paths like sheep lost on a forked trail.

I, Guang’an, am but a humble follower at the end of the ranks of Chan practitioners and reciters; through my repeated encouragement, Master Kong was thus inspired to probe the profound and compile the essentials, distilling the one from the many and pruning the redundant.
He synthesized the great achievements of all schools, thereby supplementing those who had been groping for the elephant by its parts.

Before these were fully prepared, the lamps of mind illuminated one another like a seal impressing its mark upon clay. Only then did he realize that Kāśyapa is identical to Maitreya and to hundreds of thousands of Buddhas.

That which is the intended meaning within words, and that which words cannot exhaustively convey, and that which the mind cannot reach—all of these without exception converge in the Great Sameness (*mahāsamatā*).
This can be verified nearby at Yunqi, and far back in antiquity it can likewise be verified.
Regarding this [text] in Tuṣita Heaven, the purpose of this exposition is by no means trivial.
Written on an autumn day in the Wumao year of the Wanli era by Hong Zhanzu Guang'an of Hulin.
*A Mirror for the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Fascicle One.
Composed by Guangshen, Disciple of Yunqi in Ancient Hangzhou.
△ Regarding the explanation of this sutra, it is divided into three general sections: first, the title; second, the translator; third, the main text.
First, the title:
*Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Regarding "Vajra" (Diamond):
it is the hardest among metals, most firm and sharpest, such that none of the five metals can equal it; it belongs to the Lord of Devas.
This is the treasure held by the Malla warriors; it is the mallet they wield. Prajñā (wisdom) is the mind of sentient beings, distinguished by its two aspects:
the true mark (*dharmatā*) and contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*). As for the true mark: the mind is fundamentally without marks.

Because it is far removed from delusion and falsehood, it possesses a real essence that cannot be destroyed. This markless mark is conventionally designated as the "true mark"—what is called the original face.

This is precisely what is meant by "the eyes. As for "contemplative observation" (*guanzhao*): the mind is fundamentally not an illuminator; rather, because it is far removed from conceptual discrimination, true clarity is resplendent, and beauty and ugliness manifest of themselves.

This "observation without an observer" is conventionally termed "contemplative observation. It refers to what is called "illuminating one's original face. To use an analogy: it is like the substance of a pearl and its luster;
light is emitted from the substance, and that light in turn illuminates the substance itself, such that essence and function interpenetrate.
Radiance. Neither identical nor different. As for "pāramitā," it means "reaching the other shore"; that is, reaching the other shore of the true emptiness of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Regarding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, *prajñā* is like a vajra; this refers to the function of contemplative observation.
It arises entirely based upon the essence of the true mark (*dharmatā*). Since the essence is both firm and sharp, its function is likewise firm and sharp. Because it is firm, it does not...
It is that which destroys all things; for the sake of benefit, it can destroy everything like a vajra, its edge impossible to meet.
Therefore, when it encounters existence, existence is destroyed; when it encounters emptiness, emptiness is defeated. When it touches the Middle Way, it is ground to powder and shattered to pieces.
When confronted with the fetters of ignorance and karma, they instantly melt away like ice. Whether it be saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, wherever it touches, it follows its sharp edge.
It is shattered to pieces; this is called the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.

As for the term *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, it refers to this very *prajñā* which destroys this shore of delusion and awakening, of sage and ordinary person, and reaches that other shore which is neither deluded nor awakened, vast and empty of sages.
It destroys this shore of the middle way between emptiness and existence, and reaches that other shore which is neither empty nor existent.
It is the further shore beyond insecurity; it destroys this shore of birth-and-death and nirvana.

It reaches the further shore where birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream, where sentient beings are fundamentally enlightened Buddhas, and where all phenomena are as they truly are. As the sutra says of the *prajñāpāramitā*:
"To distance oneself from something and to reach something far away" is precisely this. Yet, it is neither here nor there. It is not.
To be separated from this and to reach that is itself separation and reaching; it is not that one reaches after having been separated. As for what is spoken:

all verbal expressions are established from within ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). At the very moment of correct speaking, there is neither speech nor non-speech, neither that which can be spoken nor that which cannot be spoken;
there is no fixed dharma to be spoken. It is as the Venerable One did not see.
There is one teaching called "turning the instruction. It is not that the Tathāgata does not speak of this one teaching; it is precisely what is called "turning the wheel.
Those who reach its ultimate function act with heart and hand within the realm beyond thought, encountering the source from either side.
Seizing [the opportunity] as it arises, they act immediately, without adhering to fixed rules—just as Deshan used his staff, Linji threw his fist, Daowu brandished his ritual tablet, and Shigong...
"Drawing the bow taut" is precisely it. If one does not speak of it, it cannot serve as a teaching; if one does not employ it, it cannot serve as a school.
Although speaking and employing differ, they are both unified in this single handle of the Vajra King’s Precious Sword. As Yongjia said:
Great men, grasp the sword of wisdom; its blade is Prajñā, its flame is Vajra.
It not only emptily crushes the minds of externalists, but long ago it has already struck down the courage of the celestial Māras. Therefore, it is named the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*.
This is because within the square inch of the heart at this very moment, the Vajra Eye is inherently possessed by every person and is lacking in none. From...
From the very beginning, it is free from the marks of verbal expression, free from the marks of names and designations, and free from the marks of mental objects.

It is neither that which can disassociate nor that which is disassociated, for its nature is fundamentally disassociated. Since its nature is fundamentally disassociated, even "disassociation" does not stand.

Since disassociation does not stand, all things are completely interfused. When all things are interfused, there is not a single dharma that can be negated or established, nor is there a single dharma [to be grasped].
One may abide in it and attain it. Who is this? Who is that? Who departs? Who arrives? What can be destroyed? What cannot be destroyed?
Amidst the profuse arising of great functions, every movement is necessarily the manifestation of the absolute truth. At the tips of the hundred grasses, the radiance blazes brilliantly. Alas!

How is it that fundamental ignorance has become one's own sovereign? Whatever actions are undertaken, they invariably fall into the trap of habitual patterns, leading one to willingly endure suffering.
As for those whose aspirations are set upon the partial vehicles, let them be left aside without discussion.

Even those who fully cultivate the ten thousand practices to extensively deliver the multitude of deluded beings, and who expect to swiftly realize Bodhi—yet still perceive a birth that can be delivered, practices that can be cultivated, and a Dharma that can be attained—are, regarding the fundamental truth of non-abiding and non-attainment, more than a thousand or ten thousand miles away from it. This is so.
With this sutra, he overturns everything from its very foundation and presents it whole. He single-mindedly lashes away at deluded emotions;

directly, it is like a flash of lightning, a bright sun, an ancient mirror, or the sword Taie. There is no dream that is not startled awake, no hidden darkness that is not illuminated, no subtle detail that is not revealed, and no object that is not shattered.
He ensures that every dharma is found to be unobtainable, so that in every instance, one finally returns to the home.
Precious! Thus, the body that is originally pure is revealed. Reaching this point, how could one have expected that the self-nature is inherently pure?
How could one have expected that the self-nature is inherently complete? As for those who have departed from both extremes, how could they be described in words?
They unfold the effortless mechanism of Vulture Peak and reveal the ineffable subtlety of the Small Room (Shaoshi). They do not return...
To whom shall this sutra return? It is for this reason that the Prajñā of Huangmei is so profoundly significant. "Sutra" (jing) carries the meanings of "permanence" and "Dharma.
One might cause the sun to grow cold or the moon to grow hot, but no maras can destroy this true teaching;
this is what is called "permanence. From it the Buddha is born; from it the Dharma emerges. It is the model for all myriad virtues and the standard for all sentient beings. This is...
This is what is called the Dharma. I pray that you will take this ancient teaching of the eternal Dharma as a clear mirror to illuminate and perceive your own mind;
then, using this very mind as a lamp of wisdom, you shall shine light upon the profound meaning of the scriptures.
In this way, those who were at Huangmei and Vulture Peak in days of yore will stand resplendent before your eyes this very day. Those with the aspiration for Prajñāpāramitā should...
"Exhausting one's heart. △ Second, the translator:
Translated by Kumārajīva, the Tripiṭaka Master of the Yao Qin dynasty.
"Yao Qin" is the dynastic name; it refers specifically to Yao Xing, the later ruler. He is necessarily called "Yao" to distinguish him from the Yin (Ying) Qin of the Zhou dynasty.
During the Fu Qin dynasty of the Northern and Southern Dynasties, there was a Tripiṭaka Master who, by virtue of his mastery of the Three Piṭakas, served as a model for all sentient beings.
As for Kumārajīva—whose full name is Kumārajīvashē—the first five characters mean "Child-Life" (Tóngshòu) in this language;
"Jīva" refers to life, while "Shē" is a transliteration of the local script, combining both Chinese and Indic terms.
This refers to Kumārajīva. A "translator" (yì) is one who renders Sanskrit into Chinese. According to the *Zhou Li* (Rites of Zhou), the languages of the four quarters each had their own official;
for the north, the term was "yì. Since the scriptures came from the west, yet the term "yì" was used, it was because the northern official was also proficient in western languages.
When Dharmakāla [Móténg] first arrived, he was thus designated as a "yì," and this convention has been maintained to this day. According to...

At the age of seven, the Master accompanied his mother to a temple. There he saw an iron almsbowl and attempted to place it upon his head; suddenly, he thought, "This bowl is extremely heavy. How could I possibly lift it?
Finding that he could not bear its weight, he immediately realized that all phenomena are but mind. He became a man of vast learning and powerful memory.

No one could equal him. Because of his lofty virtue from childhood, he was called "Childhood Longevity" (Tongshou). Later, the reigning sovereign invited the Master to enter the Guanzhong region and honored him as State Preceptor.
Upon examining the old translations of the scriptures, the Master found that their meanings were frequently erroneous and deviant, and did not correspond with the Sanskrit originals.
He then assembled more than eight hundred śramaṇas and translated over three hundred and ninety fascicles of new sutras and śāstras.
These works all elucidated the source of the spirit and expounded upon their profound meanings. A few days before his passing, the Master gathered the assembly and said:
"I pray that what I have proclaimed and translated may be transmitted to future generations and circulated by all together. Now, before this assembly, I make a vow of sincerity. If..."
The transmission is without error. It shall be so that after his self-immolation by fire, his tongue will not be scorched or decayed.

On the twenty-first day of the eighth month of the eleventh year of Hongshi, he passed away in Chang’an. Upon cremation, when the wood was exhausted and the body extinguished, the root of his tongue remained solemnly intact.
Since this scripture was translated by this master, it shall be no different from the Tathāgata’s words of truth and reality.

How could one not believe it? △ Third, the main text has three parts: first, the introductory section; second, the main body of the teaching; third, the dissemination section. First, the introductory section has two parts:
first, the testimony of faith; second, the incitement. First, the testimony of faith.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
Regarding the testimony of faith: it is stated that "this Dharma was heard by me from the Buddha.
At one time, Śākyamuni was in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī, dwelling together with a great assembly who all listened to him.

Thus, the time and the master from whom it was heard are clearly verifiable; the location and the persons who heard it are likewise evident and sufficient as proof, enabling those in distant lands and other ages to understand with certainty.
Because there is no doubt regarding faith, it is called "faith as realization" (*śraddhā-saṃpratyaya*). It is also termed the "General Preface" (*sāmānya-nidāna*), because it is common to all sūtras.

If one analyzes it separately: the phrase "Thus" (*evam*) is a term that points to the Dharma; although there was no such thing prior to this, it refers back in anticipation to the Dharma of the main body (*samyak-artha*) to be explained below.
"I have heard" (*evaṃ mayā śrutam*) means that I personally heard it myself, not that I heard it from another.

Regarding people: I heard this directly from [the Buddha] himself; it was not heard by reading ancient texts. "At one time" refers to the single occasion when the teacher and disciples were assembled for teaching and listening.
It does not specify a particular year, month, or day because the divisions of time differ throughout the ten directions.

Because the calendars of the two lands differ, and furthermore, because the time for the listener may be long while the time for the speaker is short, or conversely, the time for the listener may be short while the time for the speaker is long, it is simply said to be "one time. *Buddha* means "awakening" (*bodhi*).

It refers to awakening to one's own original nature, awakening to the original nature of others, and awakening to both oneself and others such that the nature of all is fully realized. *Śrāvastī*—this...
Regarding the name "Wenwu" (聞物): because the kingdom abounded in the four virtues, its fame moved throughout the Five Indias; thus it was called Wenwu.
As for the Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍada Park: "Jeta" is the Sanskrit term, which here means "Victorious in Battle," as he was born at the time of a victorious engagement.
"Jeta" is used as the name. Now, when it is simply called "Jeta," it is for the sake of brevity in the text. "Anāthapiṇḍada" expresses his virtue; he is Sūradatta.
Since Jeta gave the trees and Anāthapiṇḍada purchased the grove, the name combines both, hence it is called the Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma.
The Sanskrit term *bhikṣu* is translated here as "mendicant" (*qǐshì*). He begs for food to sustain his body, and he begs [for the Dharma]...
Because the Dharma sustains the mind, he is also called "Terrifier of Māras," for by abandoning desire and training in the Path, he stands in opposition to Māra.

He is also called "Destroyer of Evil," for he destroys the evil of afflictions (*kleśa*) and cuts off the fetters (*saṃyojana*). He is called "Great" because he is revered and honored by celestial kings and great beings alike, as his virtue is not minor;
furthermore, there is no scripture of either inner or outer teachings that he has not mastered extensively, for his understanding is not limited.
Therefore, he transcends the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas). Because they are not inferior vessels, they are collectively termed "Great.
As for the one thousand two hundred and fifty people: first, Uruvilvā had five hundred disciples at the Fire Dragon Cave;
second, Gayā had three hundred disciples at Elephant Head Mountain; third, Nadī... [at the Śi... *Note: The source text appears to be truncated.*
The River [Vālukā] had two hundred disciples who later all returned to the Buddha; thus there were one thousand followers.
Maudgalyāyana’s relics numbered two hundred and fifty, and they too came to return to the Buddha, making a total of one thousand two hundred and fifty.

Question: The Buddha has ordained many bhikṣus beyond measure; why does he single out only these one thousand two hundred and fifty? Answer: Because of these one thousand two hundred and fifty... [text continues].
First, they took refuge in the Buddha; furthermore, they were never separated from him until his parinirvāṇa.

As for others who are scattered in the four directions, although they may have discussed these matters face-to-face across a thousand *li*, the texts were established based on their actual traces. Such is the natural course of the Dharma, just as it was among the disciples of Zhongni (Confucius).

There were approximately three thousand disciples in total, yet he singled out the seventy disciples alone because they had long resided by the Si River, supported him during his time at Chen and Cai, and frequently followed him. △ Second, the initiation [of the discourse].
At that time, when it was mealtime, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Having gone through the city in regular order and returned to his original place, he finished his meal. He then put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, prepared a seat, and sat down.
Regarding "initiation": the words of the Sage are by no means uttered casually; the arising of the teaching must necessarily depend on an occasion for its manifestation.
For example, the Lotus Sūtra emits light to inaugurate the teaching of the One Vehicle, and Vimalakīrti manifests illness to open the discourse on non-duality. Therefore, it is called "initiation."
This is also called the "Specific Introduction. Since the introductory episodes of various sutras differ—some being present and others absent—it is here specifically distinct.
Now, taking the practice of begging for food as the introductory episode serves to reveal that the physical body is but a deceptive trace, sustained by the consumption of food and drink;

whereas the Dharma-body and ultimate truth are realized through the illumination of wisdom. Sentient beings are deluded regarding the truth and cling to the deceptive, while the Buddhas rely upon the deceptive [to manifest].
To manifest the truth, he demonstrated begging for food to sustain the physical body (*rūpakāya*) and to initiate wisdom so as to give rise to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Without food, the physical body dies; without wisdom, the Dharma-body does not arise. Thus, the Sūtra says: "All Buddhas..."
And the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas—all emerge from this sutra.
"At the time of eating" refers to the morning hour (*śuna-velā*). Because it is the first part of the day, alms are easily obtained; returning to the garden occurs precisely before midday.
This follows the usual rules for the fast-day observance (*upoṣadha*). As for wearing robes: one wears those ranging from nine to twenty-five strips;
these are the *puṇya-kṣetra* (field of merit) robes. They are so called because they are fashioned like a watered field, and seeing them generates merit. As for holding an alms bowl:

it is a bowl of dark-blue lapis lazuli, which was the relic bowl of Vipaśyin Buddha offered by the Four Heavenly Kings. One must certainly wear and carry these, as laypeople take great delight in such practices.

Excessive adornment is an attachment to pleasure; the nakedness of renunciants and non-Buddhists is an attachment to suffering. Now, by abiding in the Middle Way, one remains free from these two extremes.
Furthermore, possessing a majestic presence that inspires awe and a dignified demeanor worthy of emulation, one serves as a model for others' physical conduct and inspires their reverence and faith.
How could this be merely for the sake of personal discipline? Begging for food is a *dhūta* practice. *Dhūta*... [text fragment]
It is said: "Shake off. Since the mind, which is the root of afflictions, is not easily discarded all at once, if one wishes to shake it off, it must be through personal practice.
Although practices are immeasurable, they are subsumed within twelve: namely, the forest hermitage (*āraṇya*) and the foot of a tree—these shake off the afflictions of dwelling;
the straw mat (*śayanāsana*) and the clay alms bowl—these shake off the afflictions of utensils. Namely: [the remainder follows].
Regarding the three robes: it is called "begging for food" because it shakes off the afflictions of clothing and sustenance.

This practice of begging for food not only removes greed and arrogance from afar, but also cultivates the field of merit, gathers and composes the body and mind, and keeps one free from the four wrong means of livelihood.
Therefore, the Tathāgata manifested himself as a model for future generations, so that they might know: "If even a Buddha acts in this way, how much more so should others?
He thus used to say of himself: "When the practice of *dhūta* persists, my Dharma persists; when the practice of *dhūta* perishes, my Dharma perishes. He truly valued this above all.

As for the practice of begging from house to house in sequence (*anupūrvika-bhikṣācaryā*), one does not distinguish between the pure and the impure, nor does one exclude the poor or the wealthy. By means of this—
This is because one internally realizes the principle of equality and externally forgets the characteristics of differentiation.

To "gather the robes and bowl" means to gather the *saṃghāṭī* (great robe) and put on the seven-strip robe (*saptaka*) in order to cease discursive thoughts. To "wash the feet" means to purify the physical karma. Then, one spreads out a seat and sits.
He was about to enter meditative absorption. Regarding the spreading of the seat: whenever the Tathāgata preached the Prajñāpāramitā, he would always personally spread his sitting mat.

This is because the Prajñāpāramitā gives birth to all Buddhas; it is the Mother of Buddhas. He does so to manifest reverence for the Dharma. As for the term "sitting," it refers to the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
As for why it must be the full-lotus posture, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When one sees a painting of someone sitting in the full-lotus posture, even Māra is struck with awe and fear."
How much more so for one who has entered the Way, whose body is upright and unmoving; therefore, they sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
This is not merely because the physical form is dignified and inspires respect and faith, as praised by the sages and rarely seen among non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*);

rather, it is because one can maintain this for a long duration without quickly becoming fatigued, and by thus withdrawing and collecting the body and mind, lightness and ease (*praśrabdhi*) arise readily. Among the four modes of deportment (*iryāpatha*), by means of this—
That sitting is superior is indeed for good reason. How much more so when a mirror stands facing the face—the face is naturally revealed;

when mindfulness stands facing the principle—how could the principle not be naturally revealed? Therefore, whenever the various sūtras intend to preach the Dharma, they mostly first enter meditative concentration.
The present sutra explains that suchness is immovable; yet, one may also don robes and carry an alms bowl, proceeding from door to door to beg for food—this is collectively termed *śīla* (precepts).
Spreading out a seat and sitting down is termed *samādhi* (concentration). This reveals that *śīla* can give rise to *samādhi*, and *samādhi* can give rise to *prajñā* (wisdom);
thus, *śīla* and *samādhi* serve as the initiators of wisdom. Question: The *Śrī-mālā-devī-sūtra* states: [text follows]
It is said: "The Buddha’s body is like a solid piece of diamond; it has neither raw nor cooked internal organs. What need is there for food? The *Āgama* Sūtras state:
"When the Buddha walks, he is four finger-widths above the ground; lotus flowers receive his feet, and his skin remains unstained.

What need is there for washing? Furthermore, "The Nāga is always in meditative concentration; there is no time when he is not concentrated. If this is so, why does he rest from sensory objects by sitting cross-legged?
What is the purpose of sitting? One does not know that the Buddhas' true enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is pure and subtle, fundamentally non-existent [in a literal sense].
It is only because of great compassion that, within the subsequently attained skillful wisdom, they manifest the same activities as all sentient beings in order to gather and transform them.
Therefore, entering and leaving cities, they move with effortless spontaneity while holding their alms bowls.
Washing the bowl, one proceeds spontaneously and with ease; when the time comes, it is simply so.
How could there be even a hair’s breadth of thought or calculation involved therein? This very ordinary meal is, in its full majesty, the splendor beyond kalpas.
Nanguan said, “Come and eat”; Zhaozhou said, “Go wash the bowl. There is indeed a profound flavor in these words. Furthermore, the World-Honored One sat.
It is like a great bell hanging high, waiting to resound when struck; like an ancient mirror suspended in emptiness, manifesting whatever forms appear before it.
This implicitly indicates the time for Śūnyatā to request the teaching of the Dharma.
△ Second, the Main Body of the Teaching, in four parts: First, the request by the disciple; second, the Tathāgata’s approval;
third, the disciple’s expectation to hear; fourth, the Tathāgata’s formal exposition. First, the request by the disciple, in two parts:
first, paying homage and praising the Buddha; second, formally presenting the questions. First, paying homage and praising the Buddha.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti rose from his seat amidst the great assembly;
he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is rare, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas, and well entrusts all bodhisattvas."

Subhūti looked up at the Tamer of Men; his mind waited expectantly for the inquiry. He looked down upon the various capacities of the assembly; it was precisely the moment when they were ready to hear.

Thus, he paid homage and praised the Virtuous One’s qualities as a prelude to posing his question. "At that time" refers to the time of sitting cross-legged. "Elder" (sthavira) means one who is honored both for virtue and seniority (*varga*).
Furthermore, it may refer to one whose virtue alone surpasses the multitude, or one whose seniority alone precedes others; he is also so named.
"Elder Subhūti" means "Born from Emptiness. He was given this name because at the time of his birth, his family's storehouses were entirely empty.
According to the *Record of the Western Regions*, he is said to be an emanation of the Buddha Śākyamuni appearing at the assembly of the Buddha Śikhin of the East;
he manifested as a śrāvaka to propagate the principle of emptiness. This is the universal law for all Buddhas of the ten directions. As for "rising from his seat": [text continues].
