△ Section Eight: Dispelling Doubts Regarding the Fruit of Suffering Not Yet Released from Clinging to Discourse. (Part Two). First, explaining the signless as patience;
second, exhorting the abandonment of signs to cultivate patience. (First, explaining the signless as patience. Part One: Briefly indicating the essence of patience.)
Second, the explanation through citation and establishment. First, a brief indication of the essence of patience:
"Subhūti, the perfection of patience taught by the Tathāgata is not, in fact, a perfection of patience."

The Buddha’s intention was this: "You have heard that giving the lives of beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is far superior to giving external wealth, yet you still produce the bitter fruits of rebirth in the realms of humans and devas;
therefore, it is called 'inferior. Do you not suspect that Bodhisattvas forget their own bodies for the sake of the Dharma, even to the point of sacrificing their lives or half a verse?"
This is also called ascetic practice (*duṣkara-caryā*), yet would it not also result in bitter fruit?

It is because one dwells upon signs (*nimitta*) while abandoning the body, failing to realize signlessness (*animitta*), that one invites bitter fruit. Now, the ascetic practice of a Bodhisattva is called patience (*kṣānti*).
To endure until reaching the shore of ultimate stillness and signlessness is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). Furthermore, to endure that which is not worth enduring—this is it.
The bank is not a bank; this is what is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). Since there is not even a state of stillness, how could there be a moving mind?
One directly reaches the fundamental source that is neither still nor moving. Where, then, will the fruit of suffering abide? Thus Maitreya said:
One is able to endure ascetic practices because there is goodness in asceticism; that merit is immeasurable. Such is the supreme meaning.
△ Second, the practice is performed and explained for its establishment.

Why is this? Subhūti, when in the past King Kali cut and mangled my body, at that time I had no perception of a self, no perception of a person, no perception of a sentient being, and no perception of a life-span. Why is this?

If, at the time in the past when my limbs were severed joint by joint, I had possessed a perception of a self, a perception of a person, a perception of a sentient being, or a perception of a life-span, [then I would have felt aversion].
They gave rise to anger and resentment. Subhūti, furthermore, I recall that in the past, for five hundred lifetimes, I was a rishi of patience;
during all those lifetimes, there was no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-span.
To investigate the reason why "endurance" is not "endurance": this is the practice already realized; it is a method long-tested through experience.
For example, when I was once King Kali and my body was mangled and severed, I perceived no signs of self or other.
This is the perfection of endurance (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), yet it is not the perfection of endurance. Furthermore, if one investigates the underlying principle...
Regarding the absence of a self (*anātman*): if there were a mark of self, one would necessarily give rise to resentment;
since there is now no resentment, it is sufficient to know that there is no self. Furthermore, this practice of patience is neither occasional nor accidental.
He further reflects that in the past, for five hundred lifetimes, he was a *ṛṣi* of patience, and throughout all those lifetimes, he was entirely without marks of a self or a person.
Thus, as the profound signs are refined and the mind and its objects are naturally forgotten, a habitual state is formed.
Subject and object merge into a single flavor; not only is there no suffering, but there is joy;
not only is there no anger, but there is compassion. As Maitreya said: "Free from self and from hatred, truly there is no affliction; one shares in joy and possesses compassion."
Alas! Such is the fruit of ascetic practices. Furthermore, regarding the matter of being cut and dismembered, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"I recall that in the past, I was born into a Brahmin family in the city of Potalaka in South India.
At that time, there was a king named Karapu, who was violent and cruel by nature, arrogant, and domineering. For the sake of sentient beings, at that time, I remained..."

Outside that city, he sat in silent meditative contemplation. At that time, when the trees were in full bloom during spring, the king, together with his retinue, palace ladies, and court beauties, went out of the city for an excursion. Beneath the forest trees, they indulged themselves in the five sensual pleasures.
Some of those court beauties left the king to play and eventually came to where I was. At that time, in order to sever their craving, I [acted] for them...
While I was preaching the Dharma, the king saw me and immediately conceived a malicious intent, asking me: "Have you now attained the fruit of Arhatship?
I replied, "I have not. He asked again, "Then have you attained the fruit of Anāgāmin? I replied, "I have not.
He spoke further, "Since you are young and have not yet attained these two fruits, you must still possess lustful desires."
[The King] said, "Afflictions! How can you look upon my women with such unrestrained passion?
I replied, "Great King, you should know that although I have not yet severed the fetters of desire, my inner mind is truly free from attachment. The King said, "You fool!"
"In this world there are sages who subsist on air and eat fruit; yet they still feel greed when they see beautiful forms.

How much more so for you, who are in the prime of your youth and have not yet severed your desires—how could you not be attached upon seeing such a face? I said, "Great King, that one does not crave forms when seeing them is truly not due to subsisting on air or eating fruit;
it is entirely due to fixing the mind on impermanence and impurity. The King said, "If there were someone light..."
He then gave rise to slander, saying, "How can this be called the practice of pure precepts?
I said, "Great King, if one possesses a jealous mind, that constitutes slander. I have no jealous mind; why do you say I am slandering you?
The King said, "Noble One, what is called 'precept'? I said, "Patience is called the precept. The King said, "If patience is the precept, then I shall cut off your ears."
"If you can endure this, I shall know that you uphold the precepts," [the executioner said]. He then cut off my ears. At that time, though my ears were severed, my countenance did not change.
When the king and his ministers witnessed this event, they immediately admonished the king, saying, "Such a Great Being (Mahāsattva) should not be subjected to such harm.
The king asked his ministers, "How do you know he is a Great Being? The ministers replied, "We have seen..."

While undergoing this suffering, his countenance remained unchanged. The king spoke again, saying, "I shall test him further to see whether he changes or remains the same," and immediately cut off his nose and severed his hands and feet.

At that time, the Bodhisattva had already cultivated compassion throughout immeasurable and boundless eons, out of pity for suffering sentient beings. Then the Four Heavenly Kings, harboring anger and resentment, rained down sand.
[The ground was covered with] pebbles and stones. Having witnessed these events, the king was filled with great terror.

He came to me again, knelt down for a long time, and said, "I only pray that you will take pity on me and accept my repentance. I replied, "Great King, my heart is free from anger, just as it is free from greed."
The King said, "Venerable Sir, how can this be known? I then made a vow:
"If it is true that I have no heart of anger or resentment, may this body of mine be restored to its former state. Having uttered this aspiration, my body was immediately restored. He asked:
"The Sūtras state that through the merit of a compassionate mind, one cannot be drowned by water, burned by fire, or struck by poison. [What about] kings?"
One could find no opportunity [to harm him]. Now, why was it that Kali found an opportunity to cut off his limbs? It is said:

Observe how, at the moment of making his vow, his skin remained intact; and when he offered repentance as the sand rained down, he truly became one who had attained the opportunity of a compassionate endurer (*maitrī-vādin*).
What opportunity did the king have? How great is the significance of the time of a compassionate heart! △
Second, the exhortation to cultivate patience by abandoning signs. This has two parts: first, the general heading; second, the detailed exposition.
First, the general heading: "Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should abandon all signs when generating the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Now, the Buddha’s practice of patience is thus without marks (*animitta*). Therefore, a bodhisattva should give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment by departing from marks.

*Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is the fruit of the Buddha’s wisdom; this is explained in the preceding text. "All marks" refers to the mark of self (*ātman*), the mark of dharmas (*dharma*), and the mark of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
"Departing from all marks" means being free from these three marks. One should depart from all [marks].
Regarding "arousing the mind with signs," it means one should be exhorted to arouse the mind by being free from signs, as in my own practice of signless patience (*animitta-kṣānti*).
Question: In the preceding passage, there was merely the absence of the four signs and self-clinging; why then is this called "being free from all signs"? Answer:
Observing this very point, it is evident that the wording of the preceding passage was concise while its meaning was comprehensive. This is because of the Great Mind.

When a bodhisattva is on the stage of the ground (*bhūmi*), both coarse and subtle ignorance are completely subdued. Question: Since you are speaking specifically of the practice of patience (*kṣānti*), why is it called "arousing the mind while detached from signs" (*animitta-cittotpāda*)?
Answer: Because one must first arouse the mind before beginning formal practice; during the actual practice, one’s entire being is the arousal of the mind;
and even upon reaching the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*), one does not depart from the arousal of the mind. For this reason, one is exhorted to be detached [from signs].

The arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta) permeates both cultivation and realization; it is not a matter of mere chance. II. Specific Manifestation: One should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on forms.
One should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas. One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.
If the mind dwells anywhere, it is not truly dwelling. Therefore, the Buddha said: "The Bodhisattva’s mind should not dwell [on anything]."

"Giving form" (*rūpa-dāna*) is a specific instruction and exhortation; it cites the previous teaching to urge the practice of transcending signs. Regarding "dwelling in form and giving rise to the mind," etc.:

dwelling within [form] with a sense of mastery is called the mark of self (*ātman*) and person (*pudgala*); dwelling in form and so forth as being substantially real is called the mark of phenomena (*dharma*).
"Regarding the mark of self: one should not dwell on form and so forth" means that one should admonish against generating a mind attached to marks while practicing.
"One should generate a mind that dwells nowhere" means that one should encourage the abandonment of a mind attached to marks while practicing.
"If the mind has a dwelling, it is a non-dwelling" means that if one dwells in form and so forth, one does not dwell in Bodhi; this is to enter here and exit there. Be careful.

It is a subtle matter. Therefore, when the Buddha says that the Bodhisattva’s mind should not dwell on form while practicing giving, he cites the teaching of previous Buddhas to show that one should practice by remaining free from signs (*nimitta*). Indeed, a mind that does not abide in arising is called a firm and steadfast mind.
When the mind is firm, one does not regress from bodhi. The practice of non-abiding is called "firm practice. When practice is firm, one may ascend to the other shore.
Thus Maitreya said: "To give rise to the mind of non-abandonment, to practice, and to be firm—this constitutes the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
One should cultivate that mind capable of learning."
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving in this way for the benefit of all sentient beings.
The Tathāgata has said that all marks are indeed no-marks; he has also said that all sentient beings are indeed not sentient beings.
This passage sets forth the causes for giving in order to exhort one to abandon [conceptual] marks, and cites the Buddha’s teaching to reveal original emptiness.
"One who gives in this manner" refers to giving that is free from marks. "For the sake of sentient beings, one should give in this way" refers to the cause of giving.
It is precisely because sentient beings cling to signs that they undergo the fruit of suffering. If I am able to remain free from signs, I can cause them to obtain benefit.
Yet, if while giving I still do not empty myself of the mark of self, I will instead increase their clinging to signs; in that case, where would the benefit lie?
Therefore, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, one should practice giving in this way by remaining free from signs. As Maitreya said: "Cultivate..."
One practices for the benefit of sentient beings; such is the cause by which one should recognize them.
How much more so when the Buddha taught that all marks are non-marks, and that dharmas are fundamentally empty? All sentient beings are non-sentient beings, and the self is fundamentally empty.
To exhort them to leave behind marks is nothing other than to perfect their fundamental emptiness; there is nothing added to it. Thus, Maitreya...
It is said: One should also know that sentient beings and their phenomenal characteristics are far removed [from intrinsic nature].
△ Ninth: Dispelling the doubt that the means of realization lacks substance and is not a cause. Part one: Directly dispelling the state of doubt.
Part two: Counteracting erroneous attachments. Part one: Directly dispelling the state of doubt.
Subhūti, the Tathāgata is one who speaks the truth, one who speaks reality, one who speaks as it is, one who does not speak deceptively, and one who does not speak otherwise.
The Buddha’s intention is this:
you have heard that by comparing the merits, upholding this sutra can lead to the attainment of bodhi; the gift of jewels does not equal the merit of upholding and expounding it.
Is it not the case that the fruit of certainty (*niyāma-phala*) has an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) essence?
To say it is conditioned and lacks an essence—since the term "lacking an essence" does not apply to the fruit itself—does this not fail to serve as a proof for the cause of attaining the fruit?

You do not realize that the Tathāgata speaks what is true, speaks what is real, speaks according to reality, speaks without deception, and speaks without contradiction. "True" means non-false; it refers to the teaching of the retribution of phenomena (*vipāka-dharma*) in its entirety.
To speak of great bodhi as true wisdom is to name the Tathāgata a speaker of truth; this is the meaning of reality, not falsehood.
To speak of the four truths of the Hīnayāna path by combining cause and effect is to name the Tathāgata a speaker of reality;
this is the meaning of suchness, which is unchanging. To speak of the ultimate *tathatā* that exhausts the source and bottom by combining the three emptinesses is to name [the Tathāgata]...

The Tathāgata is one who speaks according to reality (*yathāvādī*). "Different" means distinct; "not different" means that regarding the predictions for the three vehicles, as well as the names of the kalpas and lands, there is absolutely no distinction—this is what is called the Tathāgata being one who does not speak differently.
"Deceptive" means falsehood; "non-deceptive" means that because it is true, it is non-deceptive;
because it is real, it is non-deceptive; because it is suchness (*tathatā*), it is non-deceptive. Being non-different and non-deceptive, it is universally pervasive.

This is called "non-deceptive speech. The meaning is that since the Tathāgata has stated these four matters and they are all non-deceptive, how could his present statement—that upholding this sutra can lead to the attainment of bodhi—be a deceptive falsehood? Although he says that conditioned phenomena have no intrinsic substance, [it is nonetheless true].
Yet it can serve as the causal path, enabling one to realize through this the fruit of the ineffable, unconditioned reality.
Thus Maitreya said: "Although the fruit does not abide in the path, the path can act as its cause," according to the true words of the Buddhas.
That wisdom is of four kinds: the wisdom of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the wisdom of the Hīnayāna, the teaching of the Mahāyāna dharma, and all prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*).
Because these are not spoken falsely, it is as stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*: "The nature of letters is empty; there is no liberation apart from letters.
Furthermore, "reality" (*tattva*) and "suchness" (*tathatā*) are names that express qualities; they signify non-difference and non-deception, thereby excluding what is false.
Establishing the Title. △ Second, the Counteracting of Erroneous Attachments.
Subhūti, the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata—this Dharma is neither real nor false.

[The Buddha speaks thus] fearing that if they hear that one attains Bodhi by relying on words, they might then claim that Bodhi exists within the words and thus take them to be real. Fearing that they might hear...
To say that there is no bodhi within words and thereby conclude that bodhi ultimately does not exist would be false.
Therefore, to counteract such attachment, it is said: "Neither real nor false. "Neither real" means that because [all things] arise from conditions, they fundamentally lack a substantial essence;
thus, the bodhi within words is likewise merely verbal expression—how could there be a real fruit? It is like hearing the sound of the word "fire": there is only the name "fire."
Fire does not burn the mouth; how could there be a real fire that is not empty? Although words are ultimately without substance, awakening (*bodhi*) is certainly not non-existent;

how could it be empty? It is simply that [awakening] does not reside within words, yet it is not non-existent apart from words—just as fire does not reside within sound, yet it is not non-existent apart from sound. For this reason, although [it is not found] within sound...

There is no fire; yet it is not precluded that one may obtain fire by means of sound. Although there is no *bodhi* within the sūtra, it is not precluded that one may realize *bodhi* by means of the sūtra.
Thus, one should not say that there is existence within [the sūtra], nor that there is non-existence apart from words.
Only by penetrating this existence and non-existence can one abandon attachment. Therefore, Maitreya said: "In accordance with that true wisdom, one speaks of what is neither unreal nor real."
Just as one attains realization by hearing the sound [of the teaching], it is taught as an antidote to that.

However, the Sūtra does not speak of the "taught dharma" (deśita-dharma), but rather of the "attained dharma" (adhigama-dharma); this speaks of what is attained. That which is taught is precisely what is attained.
Furthermore, what is attained is actual wisdom (bhūtajñāna). Since it is taught in accordance with that actual wisdom, it is designated as "what is attained."
△ Ten: Eliminating Doubts Regarding Existence and Non-existence, as in the Case of Pervasive Presence. This section has two parts: first, eliminating doubts by citing analogies;
second, praising the merit of the sutra. First, eliminating doubts by citing analogies.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva dwells with the mind attached to phenomena while practicing giving, it is like a person entering the darkness who sees nothing at all.
If a bodhisattva practices giving with a mind that does not dwell on phenomena, it is like a person with eyes who,
when the sunlight shines brightly, sees all manner of forms.
The Tathāgata’s intention was this: “When you heard previously that all noble sages are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), will you not have doubts?
Since the unconditioned is precisely suchness (*tathatā*), and since suchness is all-pervasive, it follows that there should be no one who does not attain it.
Yet, why is it that there are those who attain it and those who do not? You do not realize that suchness has no differentiation, nor that there is any distinction between abiding and [non-abiding].”
It is merely that they do not abide in the same way. As for "dharmas," these refer to all dharmas of the six sense objects, whether empty or existent.

To abide in dharmas means that, lacking the wisdom of *prajñā*, one fails to illuminate their fundamental emptiness and instead clings to them as being real; it is due to this clinging that [one remains bound].
When one is defiled by sensory objects (*dharma*), correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) does not arise; since there is no basis for realizing the principle, one does not attain it.
If, however, one does not abide [in such objects], then correct wisdom is purified and one attains *tathatā* (suchness). Therefore, Maitreya said: "There is no wisdom that abides in phenomena."
The remainder is attained through wisdom. It is like a person entering darkness who sees nothing; this is a metaphor for how one lacking wisdom cannot attain *tathatā* (suchness).
It is like a person with eyes, when the light of the sun shines upon them, seeing various forms; this is a metaphor for how one possessing wisdom can attain *tathatā*.

Generosity is the foremost of the six perfections. To "not dwell" is the wisdom of *prajñā*. Since this non-dwelling applies here, the rest may be understood by extension;
moreover, since generosity encompasses all six perfections, not dwelling in generosity is precisely not dwelling in *prajñā*, and thus not dwelling in any of the perfections.
II. Praising the Merit of the Sūtra. This has two parts: first, a general praise of the sūtra’s merit; second, a specific elucidation thereof.
[On] Virtue. First, a general praise of the virtue of the sutra:

"Subhūti, in a future age, if there are good men or good women who are able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, then the Tathāgata, by means of the Buddha’s wisdom, fully knows these people and fully sees these people. All...
One attains the accomplishment of immeasurable and boundless merit.
Now, the ability to realize *tathatā* (suchness) arises from the purity of the mind; the purity of the mind arises from non-abiding;
non-abiding arises from wisdom; and wisdom, in turn, depends upon hearing the sutras. What are the merits of these sutras? Therefore, they must be praised.
I sigh, for this inspires me to apply myself to this in the future. Regarding those who receive, uphold, read, and recite: one first reads because one wishes to receive the text;
one first recites because one wishes to uphold the meaning. Reading with the original text before one is called "reading"; reciting without the original text is called "recitation.

Reading and recitation are the cause, while receiving and upholding are the fruit. Furthermore, as for receiving, upholding, and practicing, these involve being able to [master] both the text and the meaning in their entirety.
Receiving and internalizing [the teachings] is called the practice of dhāraṇī, and it is also termed the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

Merely reading and reciting extensively is called the practice of reading and recitation, and it is also termed the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). For if there were nothing heard, upon what could one rely for reading and recitation?

Nevertheless, that all these are called "practices" is discussed in terms of their general characteristics; it does not refer to the cultivation of the three specific wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and meditation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
Because cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*) accords with principle, it is exclusively confined to the untainted (*anāsrava*) and transcends mere recitation and retention;
thus Maitreya said: "The three kinds of dharmas consisting of names are retention through hearing and extensive exposition; cultivation arises from others and from within."
To hear this "cultivation of wisdom" is the name of this sutra. Regarding the three types: first, receiving; second, upholding; and third, reading and reciting.

Hearing the extensive exposition is itself reading and reciting; it is the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), meaning to read and recite after hearing the extensive exposition from others.
Cultivation refers to the cultivation of both receiving and upholding, as well as reading and reciting. "From others" means from another person.
"Hearing" refers to the internalizing of what has been heard; that is, upon hearing, one internally receives, maintains, and contemplates it.
One who attains this wisdom of cultivation hears the Dharma from others and then internally contemplates it, thereby attaining these two kinds of wisdom through practice.
Regarding "merit" being called immeasurable and boundless: it is inconceivable. Regarding "knowledge and vision" being said to be by means of the Buddha’s wisdom:
none other is able to know it. Regarding "accomplishment": such a person, if separated from this sutra, would lack such merit.
If that is so, is it not essential alone to read, recite, receive, and uphold this sutra? △ Second, the specific manifestation.

Its virtues are ninefold: first, the excellence of its merit as demonstrated through comparative measurement; second, the excellence of being unfathomable by other vehicles; third, the excellence of the suitability for those who are its intended audience;

fourth, the excellence of possessing the qualities that enable its transmission; fifth, the excellence of being like a stūpa wherever it resides; sixth, the excellence of attaining the fruit through the removal of hindrances;

seventh, the excellence of transcending mundane affairs and encompassing many Buddhas; eighth, the excellence of its comprehensive exposition that startles the world; ninth, the excellence of its summary which reveals profound depths.
First, the excellence of the merit is revealed through comparison.
Subhūti, if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, during the first part of the day, gave as many bodies in charity as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River;
and during the middle part of the day, again gave as many bodies in charity as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; and likewise during the latter part of the day...
One might practice giving away bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, even practicing such bodily giving for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
Yet, if there were another person who, upon hearing this sutra, did not oppose it with a mind of faith, their merit would surpass that of the former;
how much more so if they were to copy, receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain it to others!
This is the fourth comparison. Within these comparisons of the agent and the object, each has its own degrees of superiority and inferiority.

Regarding the agent of comparison, if one were to give away bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges three times daily for immeasurable kalpas, when compared to a single act of giving as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, then all the former instances of time and event are minor and inferior, while all the present instances of time and event are great and superior.
Among those who have been evaluated, those who possess faith and do not oppose [the teaching], and who especially refrain from slandering it, are superior.

Compared to those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain it to others, the former’s two benefits—of self and others—are profound and superior, whereas the latter’s non-opposition is shallow and inferior.
Previously, one compared the inferiority of the comparer with the superiority of the compared; thus, the compared was already superior.
Now, one compares the inferiority of the compared with the superiority of the comparer—how much more so, then, when comparing the superiority of the compared?
What is it like? The former is shallow and the latter is deep; they progress through successive stages of extraordinary excellence. Truly, this is divine.
A crown and a shoe are not comparable; thus Maitreya said: "Because the matter and the timing are so great, it is the most excellent among all merits.
How much more excellent, then, is the merit of this present sutra! △ Second, the fact that other vehicles cannot fathom its excellence.
Subhūti, to state it briefly: this sutra possesses inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit.
This sutra is the very Prajñāpāramitā of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) as expounded within these written words. It is "inconceivable" because:
The mind can only reach the realm of appearances; true reality is beyond appearance and thus cannot be conceived.
When the mind seeks to take it as an object, its deliberations vanish. It cannot be discussed because verbal discourse can only reach the realm of names;
since it is now beyond names, it cannot be discussed. When one wishes to speak of it with the mouth, words fail. To "extol" means to proclaim its virtues.
"Cannot be praised" means that even one's eulogies cannot exhaust it. "Cannot be measured" means that when one evaluates its virtues, they are immeasurable;
thus, even such evaluation cannot reach its limit. Therefore, know that the inconceivable is the realm of self-realization. That which cannot be measured is peerless and supreme.
The intent is that if one were to fully manifest the virtues of this sutra, they could not be exhausted; this is the essential point.
To speak of it: these are indeed inconceivable and other such merits. To realize the inconceivable is extremely difficult to measure;
it is the realm of the Buddhas, which neither the followers of the Two Vehicles nor the Bodhisattvas can attain. Thus Maitreya said: "It is not the realm of others.
How much more excellent, then, are the virtues of this present sutra! △ Third, the excellence of the intended audience.
The Tathāgata has taught this for those who have set out upon the Mahāyāna; he has taught it for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle (*anuttarayāna*).
Its essential nature and function pervade the entire *dharmadhātu*, and thus it is called "Great" (*mahā*).

It is called a "Vehicle" (*yāna*) because it is that which all Buddhas have fundamentally ridden, and because all Bodhisattvas ride upon this Dharma to reach the stage of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, it is called the "Supreme Vehicle."

The term "Mahāyāna" (Great Vehicle) encompasses both the provisional and the ultimate. Since this [text] now excludes what is provisional, it is called "supreme"; it refers to the Mahāyāna of the single reality.
The meaning is that when the Buddha preached this sutra, he did not do so for the sake of the Hīnayāna, but for the sake of the Mahāyāna;

nor did he do so for the sake of the provisional and shallow Mahāyāna, but for the sake of those who set forth upon the supreme, single-reality Mahāyāna—that is, to inspire the aspiration for... [Arhatship].
This is the capacity for the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Thus, Maitreya said: "It is taught solely in reliance upon great beings.
The Wei translation states: "It is taught for the sake of sentient beings who abide in the foremost Great Vehicle. This refers to the intended audience (*adhikāra*) of the present sutra.
How exceedingly superior this is! △ Fourth, the shared virtue of being able to transmit the excellence:
If there is anyone who can receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain it to others, the Tathāgata fully knows that person and fully sees that person;
all shall achieve immeasurable, incomparable, boundless, and inconceivable merit.
Virtue. Such persons as these shall indeed shoulder the burden of the Tathāgata’s *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
Subhūti, those who delight in inferior dharmas are attached to the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span;
they will therefore be unable to hear, receive, read, recite, or explain this sutra to others.

Those who possess this personhood are individuals of the supreme vehicle (*anuttarayāna*). To uphold, recite, and explain [this teaching] constitutes immeasurable merit for the benefit of both oneself and others;
it is the cause of *bodhi*. Therefore, Maitreya said: "It fulfills the unsurpassed realm."

"Satiation" (paripūri) has the meaning of accomplishment. "Element" (dhātu) has the meaning of cause; that is to say, the practice of the two benefits serves as the cause capable of bringing supreme enlightenment to full completion.
"Bearing the burden" means descending to transform others through great compassion and ascending to seek the goal for oneself through great wisdom.
Placing the burden of these two benefits upon the shoulders of diligence, one emerges from the midst of afflictions and birth-and-death, remaining unstuck in every thought-moment.
Until reaching Bodhi, when oneself and others are simultaneously liberated, only then is this burden cast off. Because of this, one can cause the lineage of the Buddhas not to be severed;
this is called "shouldering the burden of Bodhi. As Maitreya said: "To receive and uphold the true and wondrous Dharma.

Here, "Bodhi" refers to the true and wondrous Dharma, and "shouldering the burden" refers to receiving and upholding it. As for the question "Why is this so?", the intended meaning of the inquiry is as follows:
Why is this taught only for those of the Mahāyāna? Why is the upholding and preaching of it called "shouldering the burden of Bodhi"?

It is because those who delight in inferior dharmas (*hīnadharma*) are attached to views such as a self (*ātman*) and a person (*pudgala*), and thus are unable to hear, receive, read, recite, or uphold and preach it for others.
"Delight" means being emotionally stagnant within [those views]. "Inferior dharmas" refers to the four noble truths of arising and ceasing. Those who delight in the inferior are the Śrāvakas.
Regarding the statement that Pratyekabuddhas are "attached" and thus cannot listen or receive [the teaching], it is because those of the Hīnayāna are single-mindedly devoted to their own benefit;

they have merely emptied themselves of the attachment to a self (*ātma-grāha*), but have not yet emptied themselves of the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). This sutra, however, reveals the three kinds of emptiness.

Since the capacity [of the listeners] is shallow while the teaching is profound, the two do not harmonize, and therefore they are unable [to receive it]. Question: Those who are attached to a self cannot uphold or explain [the teaching]; this refers to the emptiness of the Hīnayāna.
[Question: You speak of "self" (*ātman*) and yet also speak of "clinging to self. Why is this? [Answer: It is said that there are many such instances in the sūtras.

First, it is for the sake of linguistic convenience; second, it is because the text is concise while its meaning is comprehensive. By merely mentioning "clinging to self," the "dharmas" are also included therein.
Therefore, it is said: "the self of persons" and "the self of dharmas. One knows that those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle are unable to uphold and expound [this teaching];
thus, those who do uphold and expound it must belong to the Mahāyāna, and must belong to the Supreme Vehicle. That they bear this burden—that they possess such merit—is it not indeed fitting?
How much more so, then, the responsibility of this present sutra! 5. Its Superiority as a Stupa Wherever It Resides.
Subhūti, wherever this sutra may be found, it should be honored by all the world—gods, humans, and asuras.
You should know that such a place is itself a stupa; everyone should pay respect, prostrate, and circumambulate it.
One should scatter various flowers and incense upon that spot.
As stated above, since the Sūtra is so exceptionally sublime, wherever it may be located, it is something that all the world ought to honor and revere.
One should know that such a place is itself a stūpa; this expresses the sense of being worthy of offerings.

Therefore, as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "If there are people who have accumulated merit by having made offerings to the Buddha in the past, wherever this sutra is located, that place shall be a stupa.
This clearly reveals that it is the very body of the Buddha; to offer worship and respect to it, how could the merit be measured? Thus, Vasubandhu says:
"Such a person will certainly accomplish immeasurable merit," and Maitreya says: "One obtains merit by respecting the [Buddha’s] body."

According to the *Zuānlíng jì* (Record of the Compilation of Spiritual Manifestations), during the Sui dynasty, in Wánglǐ Village of Xīnfán County in Yìzhōu, there was a scholar of the Xún clan whose personal name is unknown.
He inscribed characters upon the four sides of the air to the east of that village. The villagers said to him:
"What is this writing? he asked. "It is my transcription of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. "What is its use? he asked. "I shall read it with the devas," he replied.
At that time, people saw and heard him; some remained, while others vanished. It was then that torrential rain fell, and the flowing waters poured down in torrents.
Only this space, about ten feet square, remained like the floor of a hall or pavilion, completely untouched by moisture. Consequently, cowherds would frequently seek shelter there from the rain.
Although people of the time found it strange, they did not know its cause. At the beginning of the Wude era, a monk from Western India arrived; his divine appearance was quite extraordinary.
He prostrated himself at this spot, whereupon a villager asked him, "There are no temples or stupas here before you; why do you pay homage?"
"What kind of ritual is this? he asked. [The monk] replied, "Are you a fellow villager? He said, "Yes. The monk said, "You are utterly ignorant.
Here lies the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, upon which the devas have placed canopies and provided offerings without ceasing. How could you defile it to such an extent?
The villager then realized that this was the place where Master Xun had transcribed the scripture. From then on, he paved the area with bricks to honor it.
It was enclosed with a railing to prevent it from being defiled or trampled. Whenever the day for ritual fasting arrived, he would regularly make offerings there.

Those who came to gaze upon and worship it often heard the sound of celestial music. To this day, the place cannot be moistened by rain; even though it is merely an inscription in the air, it remains thus.
How much more so, then, for a scripture written clearly on paper and silk that could not be otherwise? Thus is the power of where the present sutra once resided.
How surpassing this is! △ Sixth, the superiority of attaining the fruit through the removal of obstacles.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if good sons or good daughters who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra are treated with contempt by others, it is because of their karmic offenses from previous lives which would have caused them to fall into the evil realms;
yet, because they are now treated with contempt by people in this life, their [past offenses]... [are purified].
Worldly sinful karma will be extinguished, and one shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Since the aforementioned sutra possesses such supreme benefits, why is it that there are those who uphold this sutra yet are, on the contrary, treated with contempt by others?
It is because of the causes of their past-life sinful karma, which were destined to result in falling into the evil realms, that [they experience this] now.
One gains the power to uphold this sutra, yet one is merely held in contempt by others; this is the transformation of a heavy retribution into a light experience.
Previous karmic offenses from past lives are thereby extinguished, and the causes for rebirth in the evil realms are forever stilled.
Once all obstacles are exhausted, the three virtues naturally become perfected; hence it is said that one shall attain unsurpassed bodhi. As Maitreya said: "And..."
Being far removed from all hindrances, one is further able to swiftly realize the Dharma; how superior, then, is the turning and realization of this present sutra!
Moreover, this upholding does not consist merely of grasping its words and meanings. Thus it was said of old: "Those who ascend to the stage of Buddhahood are called those who uphold this sutra.
When inhaling, one does not dwell within the aggregates or realms; when exhaling, one does not involve oneself with manifold conditions—this is to approximate such a state.
[End of section]. △ Seventh: The superiority of transcending matters and encountering many Buddhas.

Subhūti, I recall that in the past, during immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas before the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I encountered eight hundred and forty thousand *koṭi-nayuta* Buddhas, all of whom I served and made offerings to, never letting any pass in vain.
Furthermore, if there should be anyone who, in the future final age, is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra,
the merit they obtain shall not be equaled by the merit I have gained from making offerings to all the Buddhas— even a hundredth part, a thousandth, a ten-thousandth, a hundred-millionth part,
or even any calculation or analogy cannot reach it.
In the Sanskrit language, *saṃkhyeya* means "innumerable" (*wúshù*); it is the first of the ten great numbers in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
*Saṃkhyeya-saṃkhyeya* constitutes one "immeasurable" (*wúliàng*); it is the second of the ten great numbers. What is here called "immeasurable" [is thus derived from this second number].
This refers to that second [asamkhyeya-kalpa]. Furthermore, if one calculates according to the necessity of practicing for three great asamkhyeya-kalpas:
when the first kalpa was completed, he encountered the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin; when the third kalpa was completed, he encountered the Tathāgata Vipaśyin;
and when the second kalpa was completed, he encountered the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara. That the present text mentions Dīpaṃkara indicates this was during the second asamkhyeya-kalpa.
Furthermore, regarding the term *nayuta*: ten billion (*koṭi*) is a *lakṣa*; ten *lakṣas* is a *koṭi*;
ten *koṭis* is one *nayuta*, which is already one thousand billion. Now it is said that he encountered and served eight hundred and forty trillion *nayutas* of Buddhas.
Since the Buddhas were thus immeasurable, his merit was also immeasurable. And...
If one compares this with the merit of upholding this sutra in the final age, the merit of making offerings to the Buddhas does not equal even a hundredth part of it;
it does not equal a thousandth, ten-thousandth, or a hundred-thousand-millionth part, nor can it be reached by any calculation or analogy.
This is precisely because such blessings do not lead to Bodhi, whereas this sutra can lead to Bodhi. As Maitreya said: "Furthermore, it can also bring about swiftness..."
Regarding the realization of the Dharma: first, even if one were to give away treasures from the first trichiliocosm as a gift, it would not equal the merit of upholding and expounding this sutra.
Second, even if one were to give away treasures from immeasurable trichiliocosms as a gift, it would not equal the merit of upholding and expounding this sutra.
Third, even if one were to give away bodies as numerous as the sands of a single Ganges River as a gift, it would not equal the merit of upholding and expounding this sutra. Fourth, by...
The merit of giving away bodies as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers is not equal to that of upholding and expounding this sutra.
Fifth, the merit of the Tathāgata’s offerings to all Buddhas during his stages of practice (*bhūmi*) is not equal to that of upholding and expounding this sutra.
This is the ultimate limit of comparison; it is beyond analogy. Therefore, it is said: "It cannot be reached even by calculation or metaphor. This is so.
One should know that from the shallow to the deep, these five successive stages constitute the definitive comparison of the excellence of merit;

it is ultimate and exhaustive, such that nothing further can be added. Even after reaching the inconceivable stage of the karmic fruit, although there are various further comparisons, they are merely brief enumerations made according to the occasion, each intended for a specific purpose, such as resolving doubts.
This is all there is to it. It is certainly not like the previous fivefold sequence intended as a comparative praise.
Otherwise, after describing that which is most exceptionally superior, would it then be reasonable to reverse the order by citing inferior merit?
To first show reverence and subsequently display arrogance—is such a principle possible? Therefore, the virtues described in this sutra are beyond comparison; how supremely victorious they are! △
"Subhūti, if I were to fully describe the merit obtained by a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, in the final age at the end of time,
receives, maintains, reads, and recites this sutra, some people, upon hearing it, would become mentally deranged and fall into doubt."
They do not believe.
Although I have previously exhausted my words in comparison and evaluation, I have not yet fully explained it.

If I were to describe it in detail and exhaustively, speaking with complete perfection, the minds of those who hear it would become deranged and lose their composure, falling into doubt and disbelief. What can I do?
"Can it be fully explained? Question: Previously you spoke of the 'last five hundred years' where there are still those who have faith;
why do you now speak of doubt? Answer: This was merely a summary intended to startle people and to extol the excellence of the merit to the utmost.

How could this contradict the existence of faith? Nevertheless, the present sutra must necessarily be difficult to explain in full. How supremely excellent it is! △ Ninth, the general conclusion on the profound.
Profound and supreme, Subhūti!
You should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its fruit and retribution are likewise inconceivable.
What was previously compared cannot reach it; the Buddha has not yet fully explained it. If one were to state only the essentials, you should know this sutra...

The meaning is inconceivable; the retribution is also inconceivable. As for "inconceivable," it is because the meaning of the sūtra serves as the basis for the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), and since it is signless (*animitta*), how could it be conceivable?

As for the retribution, it is because it is the most supreme and wondrous Buddha-enlightenment (*buddhabodhi*); how could it be conceivable? Therefore, Maitreya said: "One accomplishes various powers and attains..."

This is the great and wondrous retribution. Although the above constitutes a proximate conclusion to the tenth type of doubt, it may also serve as a general conclusion for the preceding five sections of comparative praise.
Starting with the broad and concluding with the concise, the literary style is naturally harmonious; thus, the virtues of this present sutra are unsurpassed—how truly supreme it is!
△ 11. Severing Dwelling and Cultivating Subjugation: This is my second doubt. First, the question; second, the answer. First, the question:

At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, how should a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* dwell? How should they subjugate their minds?”
This gives rise to a doubt concerning manifestation. The doubt is as follows: Within the Tathāgata’s direct response, there are no four marks;
within the severing of doubts, the self, person, being, and life are all empty. Since there is no self, who is it that abides? Who is it that subdues? Who is it that practices?
And who is it that is free from the afflictions of doubt and attachment? Therefore, he asks: "How should one abide? How should one subdue?"
Regarding that mind: to say it is "selfless" (anātman) means it cannot be said to abide; to say it is "selfless" means it cannot be said to be subdued.
To discuss the pacification of the state while neglecting the sovereign, or to speak of defeating the enemy while abandoning the vanguard—is this not contrary to reason?
There must necessarily be a person who abides and one who subdues, yet to claim, "I can abide," or "I can subdue," while remaining unaware [of the agent]—how could this be?
Although one has departed from the realm of the consciousness of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there remains the coarse "self" that conceives of a self in relation to persons;
furthermore, having fallen into the realm of the wisdom of a Bodhisattva, there persists the subtle "self" that perceives and cognizes a self. As Maitreya said:
"To practice within the internal mind while maintaining the notion of being a Bodhisattva constitutes an obstruction to the mind and contradicts the path of non-abiding. II. The Response.

The Buddha told Subhūti: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they should give rise to this thought: 'I should bring all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa.
Yet, after having brought all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, not a single sentient being has actually been brought to parinirvāṇa. Why is that? Because if a bodhisattva..."
If one possesses the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, then that one is not a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma whatsoever that gives rise to the thought of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding the "self" that I respond to, there is the nominal self and the true self. As for the nominal self, it refers to oneself when addressing others;
it is a provisional designation called "self. As for the true self, it is the originally existent nature—the self that is eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
To destroy that subtle [nominal] self, one must necessarily rely on the true self. Yet, in order to manifest the true self, one does not depart from the nominal self. Therefore...

"Only when one says 'I should' does the pair become complete. "I should bring all sentient beings to nirvāṇa, yet in reality there are no sentient beings who attain nirvāṇa"—this directly reveals the absence of an object to be saved.

"If one possesses marks such as self or person, one is not a bodhisattva"—this conversely reveals the absence of a person capable of saving. "In reality, there is no dharma called 'arousing the mind'."
This collectively reveals that there is no dharma of subject or object. This is the path of non-abiding. It is the descent without one who descends;

it is the self without a self. This is the mind that a Bodhisattva ought to give rise to. If one perceives an external object to be saved while maintaining an internal subject that saves, such that subject and object remain distinct, yet claims "I abide" or "I descend," this is what Maitreya calls "preserving the self."
A bodhisattva would then deviate from the path of non-abiding; it is a mind that a bodhisattva ought not to give rise to.
Why do you create obstacles for yourself within the state of equality and non-abiding, where not a single dharma can be apprehended?
Furthermore, when I respond to the "I," this "I" and the mind that is about to arise are distinct in name but identical in essence. For this mind is...
The True Self. The True Self is precisely this mind; it differs from the "name-self" (nāma-ātman) only in that the former encompasses both [the name and the substance].
△ Section Twelve: Dispelling the Doubt that Because There is a Cause for Buddhahood, There Must Be Bodhisattvas. Part One: Raising the Doubt as a Question. Part Two: Resolving the Doubt as an Answer.
Part Three: Confirming the Answer. Part Four: Repeatedly Clarifying the Point. First, raising the doubt as a question.
Subhūti, what do you think? Did the Tathāgata, while in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, obtain any dharma called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?

The Tathāgata’s intention is this: when you hear that there is truly no dharma by which one gives rise to the bodhicitta, do not misunderstand its meaning by thinking that there is absolutely no bodhisattva whatsoever, nor should you doubt me regarding my time with Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
To practice the bodhisattva path—does this imply that there is a "bodhisattva" who exists? Consider this carefully.

Did the Tathāgata attain awakening through some dharma while with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, or did he attain awakening through the absence of dharma? You should examine this and reach a definitive conclusion. Question:
Previously it was stated that "in truth, there is no dharma by which one awakens to bodhi," yet now it is said that there *is* a dharma. How can these two statements be reconciled?
Regarding the attainment of Bodhi: while both the preceding and following passages speak of "Bodhi," it would be more appropriate here to say, "I doubt that there is Bodhi.
Why, then, does it say, "I doubt that there is a Bodhisattva"? It is said: In the phrase "one who has previously aroused the Bodhicitta," the character *zhě* (者) refers to the person.
It is still said that "in reality, there is no dharma. The bodhisattva who has resolved to attain enlightenment is, in the present text, the Tathāgata;
that is, the bodhisattva within the causal stage. Moreover, whether one attains *bodhi* or does not attain *bodhi* also pertains to the person.
Therefore, this remains a point of doubt within the treatise. △ Second, resolving the doubt as an answer.
"No, World-Honored One. As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no dharma by which the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara."
The previous Buddha said "no," and now the answer is "no. Doubt has been resolved. To understand the meaning of what the Buddha taught is precisely the meaning of the inconceivable *tathatā*.
There is no dharma that attains *bodhi*; there is neither a mind capable of attaining it nor an objective realm attained.
It is tranquil and signless, free from all conceptual discrimination; one attains non-attainment and is thus spiritually awakened.

The mind stands firm and upright. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "When both the seer and the seen are entirely eliminated, yet the true vision is not destroyed—this is called one who possesses true vision.
How could it be that the utter cessation of all things, termed "non-existence," constitutes the arousal of bodhicitta?
△ Third, the seal of confirmation upon his answer.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Subhūti. In truth, there is no dharma that the Tathāgata has attained as 'anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi'."
He repeats these words as a seal to confirm this profound point: "In truth, there is no dharma by which one attains bodhi.

This means that at the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I realized that not a single dharma could be attained. If one attained bodhi through the practice of giving, what need would there be for precepts, patience, and so forth?
If one attained bodhi through a preceding thought-moment, what need would there be for subsequent thought-moments? Every practice is empty; every mind...
There is no abiding. In truth, there is no dharma by which one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. △ Fourth, reiterating and clarifying:

Subhūti, if there were any dharma by which the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, then Dīpaṃkara would not have bestowed upon me this prediction: "In a future age, you shall become a Buddha, named Śākyamuni."
"O Bhikṣuṇī, because there is truly no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
for this reason Dīpaṃkara Buddha conferred upon me the prediction, saying: 'In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.'"

This explains in detail, by means of the bestowal of prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), that no dharma can be apprehended. "Bestowal" (*śu*) means to give; "prophecy" (*ji*) refers to a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*).
It is the act of predicting in advance—concerning the name, the eon, and the buddha-field—such that there is no error. Furthermore, there are four types:

first, the prophecy bestowed upon those who have not yet resolved their minds toward awakening, because it is observed that they will certainly resolve their minds in the future and attain bodhi. Second, the [prophecy] bestowed immediately upon resolving the mind...

He received a prophecy regarding his mind, because he dwells on the stage of non-retrogression with a heart of compassion. He received a prophecy regarding his three secrets, because the six perfections were about to be fulfilled.
The devas and nāgas doubted that he would attain bodhi, so the Buddha subsequently conferred the prediction upon him to sever the doubts of the multitude.
Because the Bodhisattva did not yet know this, he received the prediction of the fourfold patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

That is to say, by now spreading his hair to cover the mud, relying on a mind still subject to outflows (*sāsrava-citta*), he obtained the prediction of non-arising; for it was clearly bestowed upon him in the midst of the great assembly.
"If there were any dharma by which one attains bodhi, then one would not receive the prediction"—this is the contrapositive explanation. It means that if there were any dharma to be attained, then...
If there is an internal mind capable of attaining and an external object to be attained, this is utterly contrary to the quiescent, signless Bodhi;
thus, one cannot receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). The statement, "Because in reality there is no dharma by which one receives the Buddha's prediction," etc., is a further explanation.
It means that when both emptiness and multiplicity are forgotten, and both subject and object are stilled, at the point where delusive confusion is exhausted, true wisdom [arises].
Manifesting before one’s eyes, it perfectly accords with the fundamental mind; thus, the Buddha acts as a witness, and in this sense, one may say "attainment" occurs.
Yet, how could there truly be a single dharma that is attained? Know therefore that there is no bodhi; thus, one receives the prediction of attaining bodhi.

One should know that it is precisely because there is no dharma that one is called a bodhisattva. Hence it is said: "In truth, there is no dharma by which one gives rise to the bodhicitta. Why is this so?
Is it because there is no Bodhisattva that you harbor doubt? Furthermore, Dīpaṃkara did not bestow the prediction (vyākaraṇa) in the present, but bestowed it for the future.
This is because although Kāśyapa’s practice was without attainment, he had not yet fulfilled its measure or reached its ultimate limit.
As it says regarding Maitreya: "The prediction is bestowed at a later time. Thus, Dīpaṃkara’s practice was not supreme; this precisely reveals the nature of causal practice.
This is the Bodhisattva. △ Thirteen:
Dispelling the Doubt that Without Causes There Would Be No Buddha-Dharma, in three parts: First, dispelling the doubt that there is no Buddha; Second, dispelling the doubt that there is no Dharma;
Third, illustrating the true Buddha-Dharma. First, dispelling the doubt that there is no Buddha.
Why is this? "Tathāgata" means the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.
Subhūti, if someone were to say that the Tathāgata has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, in reality there is no dharma whatsoever that the Buddha has attained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

As for the question "Why is this so?": the intention is to ask whether, having heard that there is no bodhi to be attained, you might doubt that the fruit of the Dharma is called bodhi, and that only upon its realization is one named a Buddha; and if there is no bodhi, would it follow that there is no Buddha?

To not understand the Tathāgata is to not understand the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. True suchness is primordially present as the Buddha, just as pure gold is primordially present.
Therefore, it is not non-existent. Since the Buddha is itself bodhi, there is simply nothing to be attained.
If anyone were to say that the Tathāgata attains bodhi, this person speaks untruthfully.
Subhūti, in reality, there is no dharma by which the Buddha attains anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. As Maitreya says: "Bodhi is that practice, and so forth."
This refers to the non-attainment of the fruits of bodhi and the preceding causal practices of a bodhisattva. To explain this in detail:

regarding the meaning of "all phenomena are suchness" (*dharmāḥ tathatā*), "all phenomena" refers to facts, while "suchness" refers to principle. This is the state where fact and principle are identical, like a vessel and its gold being entirely one;
it signifies that the entire substance is non-dual. This corresponds to the person who is free from discursive thought, the original enlightenment of all Buddhas.
The Pure Dharma-body. As stated in the *Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Lion’s Roar of Queen Śrīmālā): "The Dharma-body pervades all places—within all sentient beings and all lands;
throughout the three periods of time, it exists without exception, yet it has no form or characteristic that can be apprehended. This is precisely the meaning [of the present passage].
Just as gold mixed with ore is called a "sentient being in affliction," when the ore is smelted away and pure gold remains, it is designated as a "Buddha of Bodhi."
Pure gold exists inherently; how could the Buddha be non-existent? The Buddha is itself bodhi; why then say it is "attained" anew? 2.
Dispelling Doubts Regarding Non-existence:
Subhūti, as for the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata, within this there is nothing...
It is real and not false; therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are Buddha-dharmas.
Subhūti, that which is called "all dharmas" is precisely not all dharmas; it is for this reason they are called "all dharmas."
The Buddha’s intention was this: Your previous doubt that there is a dharma to be attained through causal practice falls into the attachment to real existence;
therefore, I said that no dharma attains bodhi. If you further doubt that bodhi cannot be attained, you will again fall into the attachment to nihilism.
You do not know that the Tathāgata neither attains bodhi nor does not attain bodhi; it is simply that...
The enlightenment thus attained is neither real nor unreal. "Neither real" means it is not a form, not a sound, and lacks any manifold substantiality or obstruction;
therefore, Maitreya said that its characteristic is not that of being substantially existent. "Not unreal" means:
It does not depart from form and sound, yet possesses a true essence. It is like a reflection in a mirror, which has no substance of its own and is entirely the luminosity of the mirror;
or like the luminosity of the mirror, which is without characteristics, yet takes form and so forth as its characteristics.

As the *Awakening of Faith* states, both the untainted and ignorance are identical in their nature and characteristics to True Suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, Maitreya said: "That is the characteristic of non-characteristic," because it is spoken of as being non-deceptive.
This is because, being unreal, it is not identical to all phenomena; yet, because it is not false, it is not separate from all phenomena.
Therefore, all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma, for there is nothing that is not the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
As for "it is not identical to all phenomena," this means that while form (*rūpa*) and so forth are indeed True Suchness, they are not the obstructive, substantial phenomena of form and so forth.
Furthermore, because True Suchness (tathatā) has no form or other such qualities, it is perfectly pervasive and pure, leaving no room for anything else.
For this reason, that which is called "all phenomena" (sarvadharma) is precisely the self-nature of the dharma of True Suchness;
thus, it is the totality of all things as being identical with their very nature. As Maitreya said: "This dharma is the dharma of all Buddhas; it is the essential body and characteristic of all."
Three analogies illustrate the true Buddha-dharma.

Subhūti, it is as if there were a person with a large body. Subhūti said, “World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata speaks of a ‘large body,’ that is not a large body; it is merely called a ‘large body.’”

What was previously stated as "Tathāgata" refers to the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena; thus, this Buddha is not non-existent. Furthermore, it was stated that "all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma";
thus, these dharmas are not non-existent. Moreover, the meaning of the suchness of all phenomena is precisely that all phenomena are the Buddha-dharma;
thus, the Buddha and the Dharma are not different. However, I have yet to ascertain which specific things constitute the Buddha-dharma.
Regarding the true essence, how can one say it is neither non-existent nor different? Therefore, it is elucidated by means of a simile: "For example, a person’s body is large and tall.
This points to the pure *dharmakāya* that transcends all entanglements. Thus, Śūnyatā-vibhava expressed his intention, saying:
"When the Tathāgata speaks of a person’s body being large and tall, it is not a large body; it is called a 'large body. That which is 'not a large body' is..."
The conditioned body is what is called the "great body"; this refers to the unconditioned body. As Maitreya said:
"Based on that Dharma-body Buddha, the metaphor of the great body is taught; for this body is free from all obstacles and pervades all objects."
Because it possesses both merit and a great essence, it is called the "Great Body" (*mahākāya*). That which is "non-body" is itself the body; therefore, it is called "non-body.

As for "all obstacles," this refers to the two obstacles: the afflictive (*kleśa*) and the cognitive (*jñeya*). Its essence is as vast as water, and its merits are as vast as the eight qualities of water.
Their essence and characteristics are neither identical nor different, for they all pervade the *dharmadhātu*. Thus...
Regarding the statement "one of great body," the intended meaning is that when the Tathāgata speaks of a human body being large and tall, he is manifesting the pure *dharmakāya*.
This is because it is free from all obstacles, pervades all places, and both its essence and its characteristics are vast. When these four meanings are combined, it is called "the great body.
As for "that which is not a body is itself the body," this means it is not a conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) body; rather, it is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) body.
Therefore, when it is said that there is "no body," this is merely using negation to reveal the Dharma-body. This is the true Buddha and the true Dharma;
it is not only not non-existent, but furthermore, it is not different [from the Buddha]. When one is free from obstructions, it appears as if something is attained;

yet, by being free from obstructions, one perfects what was originally possessed. Thus, there is attainment, yet no attainment. Why, then, do you harbor doubts regarding attainment and non-attainment?
△ Section 14: Dispelling the Doubt that There Are No Beings to Deliver and No Land to Adorn (3). First, the refutation of the thought of delivering beings;
second, the refutation of the thought of adorning the land; third, the explanation establishing the Bodhisattva. First, the refutation of the thought of delivering beings.
Subhūti, it is the same for a bodhisattva. If one were to say, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to final nirvāṇa," then that person would not be called a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma that can be named a bodhisattva.
Therefore, the Buddha has said that all dharmas are without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-principle.

The Buddha’s intention was this: my previous statement that there is truly no dharma that gives rise to the bodhicitta was merely intended to sweep away the notions of self and person (*ātman-pudgala*), not to negate the existence of the bodhisattva. You might now suspect that if there is no self or person, then there is no bodhisattva;
and if there is no bodhisattva, who is it that delivers sentient beings and who is it that adorns the buddha-lands? You do not realize that the bodhisattva is [empty of] self.
To deliver [beings] is called "delivering beings. To have no adornment is called "adorned lands. To have no bodhisattva is called a "bodhisattva. It is also as the Buddha has said:

that which is not a body is called a "great body. If one forms the thought, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," then one is not called a bodhisattva. Why? Because in reality, there is no dharma that is named "bodhisattva."
Now, if there is a mind that can deliver and beings who are delivered, one would not surpass those dharmas. How, then, could there be a bodhisattva?
For this reason, the Buddha taught that all dharmas are fundamentally without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span.

It is called "non-existence. How could one forcibly cause it to be non-existent? Question: Among the previous twelve doubts, the doubt regarding the non-existence of Bodhisattvas has already been severed.
Why is there doubt again now? Answer: This [doubt] arises together with the twelve others within the eleventh [section], but it is only now that it is severed.
Thus, we know that while their arising is simultaneous, their severance must follow a sequence; they are not redundant.
Furthermore: △ Second, the refutation of thoughts regarding the adornment of the Buddha-land.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva should form this thought: "I shall adorn the Buddha-land," he is not called a bodhisattva.
Why is this? As the Tathāgata has said: "That which is called the adornment of Buddha-lands is not actually an adornment; it is merely named 'adornment. Maitreya said:
"If one does not realize the true Dharma-realm, yet gives rise to the thought of saving sentient beings and purifying a Buddha-land, such a production of mind is itself an inversion.
To think 'I shall adorn [the land]'—this production of mind is an inversion. It is not an adornment. It is... [not an adornment]. It is... [merely named 'adornment']."
This is called "Adornment," for it realizes the true Dharma-realm. Question: How does this differ from the sixth adornment? Answer:

The former addresses the doubt that there is grasping where there is no grasping; the present addresses the doubt that there is a person where there is no person. While the adornment is the same, the doubts are entirely different.
△ Third, the explanation of the accomplishment of the Bodhisattva.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva penetrates the non-existence of self and dharmas, the Tathāgata calls him a true bodhisattva.
To harbor thoughts of adorning oneself with the means of delivering sentient beings as described above is a perversion; such a one is not called a bodhisattva.
Yet, what must be the case before one can be called a bodhisattva? The Buddha then provides a clear and definitive resolution, saying: "If one penetrates..."

One who realizes the non-existence of self and phenomena is called by the Tathāgata a true Bodhisattva. Since self and phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, one speaks of "seeking to penetrate" them;
yet if there is no penetration, then "I can deliver," "I can adorn"—such sentiments arise within the midst of quiescent equality.
To realize this, then deliverance is itself non-deliverance, and adornment is itself non-adornment; one accords with the nature in its pure stillness.

The manifestation of merit: though the myriad practices are manifold, when the dust of transgressions is repented away, it does not stand; when the one truth is concentrated and still, all virtues shine forth brilliantly.

Throughout the day one is a bodhisattva, yet ultimately there is no bodhisattva at all. This is what is called a true bodhisattva. How, then, can there be any doubt regarding the lack of human form in his majestic transformation?
