“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye? “Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the divine eye.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye? “Yes, World-Honored One...”
“Venerable One, the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*). Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*)?
“Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye. “Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*)?
“Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye.”
The Tathāgata’s intention was this: "You have heard that there is nothing to be delivered in delivering, and nothing to be adorned in adorning;
one is called a bodhisattva only when one does not perceive self or other dharmas. Will you not then doubt that the Buddha also does not perceive any dharmas?

Therefore he asked, "What do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye (māṃsa-cakṣus) or not? As for the fleshly eye, it refers to the four sense-objects: form, odor, flavor, and tangibility.
Flesh. It is the organ of ultimate purity that relies upon flesh and issues forth from flesh; that which possesses the capacity for visual perception is called the "fleshly eye" (*māṃsa-cakṣus*).
However, its function is limited to observing forms within its range. As for the "divine eye" (*divya-cakṣus*), it refers to that which is produced through the practice of meditative cultivation.
Relying on the scope of the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), one perceives external objects; because these are accomplished through visualization, one is able to see forms beyond obstructions.
The wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) refers to fundamental ultimate wisdom (*mūla-paramārtha-jñāna*), which illuminates the principle of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

The dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) refers to subsequently attained provisional wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-saṃvṛti-jñāna*), which illuminates differentiated phenomena. The Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*) is wisdom that reaches its ultimate limit and illumination that is perfectly complete. The first two...

It is common to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). The latter two are absent in the *śrāvakas*. The *bodhisattvas* lack only the Buddha-eye, yet they differ from one another in their respective degrees of depth.
Only the Buddha is fully endowed with the former four; each is uniquely superior and is called the Buddha-eye.
Beyond the Buddha-eye, there are no other four eyes. It is like the four rivers entering the ocean: once they have entered, the individual rivers can no longer be discerned.
Therefore, the fleshly eye of an ordinary person sees only what is within its range; the divine eye sees what is beyond that range. The Buddha’s fleshly eye sees countless worlds;
the divine eye of those of the Two Vehicles sees only one great trichiliocosm, whereas the Buddha’s divine eye sees as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
The wisdom-eye of those of the Two Vehicles illuminates only the emptiness of the self, while the Bodhisattvas on the stages likewise all [illuminate] it partially.
[The Buddha] realizes the Buddha’s eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*), which perfectly illuminates the three emptinesses and penetrates through to the true nature.

The Dharma-eye of a Bodhisattva does not exhaust all that is known and possesses its own limitations; the Dharma-eye of a Buddha, however, knows all things with complete purity—there is no phenomenon it does not know and no being it does not deliver.

Therefore, it is said that each and every one is uniquely supreme. The intent is that the previous statement regarding the Bodhisattva’s deliverance of sentient beings [is now contrasted with the Buddha’s].
Regarding the adornment of the buddha-field: it is simply the departure from the dualistic discrimination of subject and object; therefore, it is said that one does not perceive self or other.
Why, then, should one doubt that the Buddhas lack the eye of true wisdom? Thus Maitreya says: "Although they do not see all phenomena, it is not that they lack the eye that cognizes objects."
This refers to the five eyes that illuminate and comprehend all phenomena. △ Second, regarding the wisdom and purity of mind as known by the objects of cognition:
"Subhūti, what do you think? Are the grains of sand in the Ganges River what the Buddha calls 'sand'? As...
"Yes, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata has spoken of these as grains of sand. "Subhūti, what do you think?

If there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in a single Ganges River, and if there were as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers—would they be many?
"Very many, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Subhūti: "In that many lands..."
Among all sentient beings, however many kinds of minds there may be, the Tathāgata knows them all. Why is this?
The Tathāgata has said that all minds are "no-minds," yet they are called "minds. For what reason? Subhūti, the past mind cannot be apprehended;
the present mind cannot be apprehended; and the future mind cannot be apprehended.
First, it refers to the number of grains of sand in a single river; second, it refers to the number of rivers equal to that number of grains of sand;
third, it refers to the number of world-systems equal to that number of grains of sand. Within all those lands, there are sentient beings;

regarding the various mental intentions of those sentient beings—that is, such a multitude of mental states—the Tathāgata’s five eyes can know them all. Therefore, Maitreya said: "The Buddhas possess five kinds of reality."
This is because one perceives those [minds] as inverted. Why is this so? Because the Buddha taught that all such minds are not the true mind;

they are called "inverted minds. Thus Maitreya said: "The various kinds of inverted consciousnesses, because they are separated from true mindfulness and do not abide in that true wisdom, are therefore called inverted.
Furthermore, if one investigates the reason why they are inverted, it is because they have already departed from...
According to ultimate wisdom, these various minds are illusory and devoid of substance. If one seeks them in the past, the past has already ceased;
no substance can be found. If one seeks them in the present, the present does not abide; no substance can be found. If one seeks them in the future...
The future has not yet come; it possesses no substantiality that can be apprehended. Since the three periods of time are entirely empty, to take the void for reality is called "inversion.
Thus, all minds are but shadows of inverted illusions, while pure wisdom is the light of the mirror reflecting things as they truly are.
When this light encounters these shadows, even the finest details are exhausted, and beauty and ugliness are revealed with clarity. Who would say that the Tathāgata does not see them?
Is this the Dharma? Question: The eye can only see, while the mind can be said to know. Why, then, are the five eyes called "knowing"? Answer:
Because the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are not two distinct entities; they cannot be conceived of as being separated by delusive thoughts.

“Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would that person, by reason of this, acquire much merit? “Indeed, World-Honored One, that person would acquire very great merit by reason of this.”
The Tathāgata’s intention was this: "You have heard that the mind is inverted and entirely unattainable; will you not then doubt that merit arises dependent upon the mind?
Since the mind is inverted, merit would also be inverted. Being inverted, it is not wholesome; what benefit is there in cultivating it?"
Therefore, he asked: "In your opinion, what do you think? Would this person, by reason of these causes and conditions, obtain much merit?
"This person" refers to the one who gives away treasures filling the world-system; it means:
would this person who gives such treasures, by virtue of the nature of that cause of giving, obtain much merit? Śūnyatā-janman (Empty-Born) then said: "As for this person who gives treasures..."
By means of this cause and condition of giving, the merit is not merely great; one attains exceedingly vast merit.

The underlying intent is that causes and conditions lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), and it is precisely through this lack of intrinsic nature that they become untainted (*anāsrava*); therefore, it is said to be "exceedingly vast.
As for the phrase "merit is non-existent" in the subsequent text, this refers to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of these very causes and conditions. △ Second, the repeated explanation.
It is so, Subhūti. If merit were substantial, the Tathāgata would not say that one gains a great deal of merit.
Because merit is insubstantial, the Tathāgata says that one gains a great deal of merit.
"If merit had substantial reality, the Tathāgata would not say that one gains much merit"—this is an *inversion* (reductio ad absurdum).
"Because merit lacks substantial reality, the Tathāgata says that one gains much merit"—this is a *direct explanation*.

"Having substantial reality" refers to those who do not realize that the nature of causes and conditions is empty, who grasp at things as real, and whose giving dwells upon signs (*nimitta*). "Merit lacks [substantial reality]" refers to those who have realized...

Conditions and causes lack intrinsic nature; thus, one does not give rise to attachment. This is the merit of non-abiding. Therefore, Maitreya said: "The root of the Buddha’s wisdom is not a merit based on inversion.
Because the mind and consciousness dwell in attachment, inversion is produced; if one relies upon this to cultivate merit, that too becomes inverted.
The Buddha’s wisdom is non-abiding and far removed from inversion; it is upon this that one should base the cultivation of merit."

Thus, it becomes true reality (*tattva*). Since true reality accords with the nature (*dharmatā*), it is indeed most abundant. If that is so, one should not cultivate the merit of a deluded mind dwelling in signs;
why then should one not cultivate the merit of wisdom that is free from signs? Question: If the nature of merit is empty, then merit is indeed most abundant.
If the nature of the deluded mind is also empty, should delusion likewise be most abundant? Answer: It is the single mind of the Dharma-realm (*ekadharmadhātu-citta*).
Originally they do not abide; originally they are empty and quiescent. The Buddha’s wisdom is empty and does not abide, conforming to the fundamental nature;
therefore, awakening to the emptiness of nature brings forth immense merit. The deluded mind is inverted, abiding and not empty, thereby contravening the fundamental nature.
Therefore, when one awakens to the emptiness of nature, the deluded mind is entirely exhausted; how can they be treated as mere equals? △ Seventeen:

Therefore, when it asks "What is the meaning of 'complete'? it refers to the sense of "accomplishment. As for the "form-body" (*rūpakāya*), it refers to the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*).

Form (*rūpa*) is like the clarity of a mirror; its essence is fundamentally not a reflection. Thus Maitreya said: "The ultimate essence of the Dharma-body is not that body of marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
Because it is not the accomplishment of marks, it is not that Dharma-body. He further stated: "This is called the 'body of form endowed with all aspects' (*rūpakāya-samanvāgata*).
This is because the body of form is not separate from the Dharma-body; thus, even the marks and signs are not non-Buddha, just as in the case of a mirror.
Only by clarifying that there is no object can an object be manifested; yet the manifested object does not depart from the mirror. As Maitreya said: "It does not depart from the Dharmakāya.
Since those two are not non-Buddha, he speaks again of "accomplishment" (siddhi). Furthermore, there is neither duality nor existence.
Viewed in this light, it is acceptable to say that the Dharmakāya manifests as the Rūpakāya; however, one must not cling to the Dharmakāya as a mere phenomenon.
It is not permissible to view the physical body [as the Buddha]. However, it is permissible to view the physical body as the Dharma-body.

It is not permissible to cling to the physical body as being merely the physical body. Is it that the Dharma-body is the Buddha, while the marks and signs are not? △ Second, resolving the doubt that the Buddha is characterized by various marks.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of his possession of the various marks? “No, World-Honored One.
The Tathāgata should not be seen by means of his possession of the various marks. Why is this? What the Tathāgata calls the possession of the various marks is itself no possession;

The marks refer to the thirty-two major marks. Beginning with the white tuft of hair on the head and ending with the wheel-mark on the feet—these are the great marks.
One should not argue that they are not identical to the names and so forth; this is entirely in accordance with the previous meaning.

Indeed, while the Tathāgata was in the causal stage, he cultivated the hundred blessings through wondrous wisdom that accords with the nature of reality, and only then did he manifest a single mark. Now, when people touch his crown...
Reaching even to the heels—these signs of extreme meager merit and extreme folly are all brought about by the accumulation of hundreds of evils practiced over many lifetimes.
Thus, observing the fruit to verify the cause, one should indeed be fearful.

second, revealing the correct view. First, refuting divergent views:
"Subhūti, do not say that the Tathāgata has this thought: 'I shall teach some Dharma. Do not hold such a view."
[The Buddha] said: "Reflect on this. Why? If anyone says that the Tathāgata has preached any dharma, they slander the Buddha, for they fail to understand what I have taught.
The Buddha’s intention was this:
"You have heard that the Buddha is named for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); could it be that you now think he also produces sound based upon form?"
Since there is no form upon which it depends, how could there be a sound capable of being produced? One might then doubt how one who has no body can preach the Dharma.
This is not to realize that this refers to the attachment that the Tathāgata has something to preach. Therefore, it says, "Do not say," and "Do not do.
Why must these words be repeated as a warning? The commentary explains: if a person says that the Tathāgata...
To say that there is a dharma taught is to slander the Buddha, for one cannot understand the dharma I have taught.
It is not merely a matter of failing to understand; it constitutes slander. Therefore, I caution you not to harbor the notion that there is a dharma taught.
Question: In the preceding passage, "this is called the fulfillment of the form-body" (rūpakāya), you have just revealed the body that is no-body. Why then...
[The Master] turned and addressed the doubt regarding "preaching the Dharma with no body," saying: "This, along with the previous doubt, both reside within the third doubt; they arise simultaneously.
Therefore, the former doubt was severed first, and this doubt is severed afterward. It does not follow from the preceding text. Question:
"Since the former doubt has already been severed, one should have awakened to the subsequent doubt; there would be no need to sever it again. Answer: "In principle, it is so."
One knows this because of that; yet, since both doubts arise simultaneously, they must necessarily be severed one after the other.
The Buddha, concerned for the final age and fearing that people would not understand, was therefore most earnest and repetitive in every matter.
△ Second, showing right view.
Subhūti, the one who preaches the Dharma has no dharma to preach; this is called preaching the Dharma.
Now, to have something to preach is to slander the Buddha and to lack understanding. How must one act to achieve correct understanding?
However, when one preaches the Dharma, there is no dharma that can be preached; this is called preaching the Dharma. It is like a silent, empty valley:
when a sound comes, an echo arises, yet there is no echo that can be called an echo; it is merely what is termed an "echo. Although it responds, there is no thought of responding;
although one speaks, there is no mind that preaches the Dharma. Because there is neither thought nor mind, [it is so].
One is merely able to respond and speak. What dharma is there that can be spoken? Therefore, Maitreya said: "As it is with the Buddha, so it is with the Dharma;
the two distinctions of what is spoken do not depart from the dharmadhātu. Regarding the phrase "the two distinctions," this refers to both the teaching and its meaning.
Regarding "having no self-characteristic," this means that the teaching arises from causes and conditions; that which is born of conditions is empty of intrinsic nature.
It is said that no self-nature can be apprehended. The meaning is that not only is the Buddha’s body a "bodyless body," but the Buddha-dharma is also a "dharmaless dharma.
It is entirely the single true Dharma-realm, wherein no self-characteristics whatsoever can be apprehended.
If this is so, why do you harbor doubts regarding what has been taught? Question: The third doubt concerns the fifth [section].

The doubt regarding the seventh [chapter] and the present doubt both state that there was no teaching. How do they differ? It is said: the third doubt concerns whether Kāśyapa’s transformation body had a teaching;
the fifth doubt concerns whether the realized wisdom of Dīpaṃkara could be taught; the seventh doubt concerns whether the Buddha had different teachings;
and the present doubt concerns how there could be a teaching when there is no body. Since the doubts are not the same, the judgment that there was no teaching is clear. Please examine this closely.

At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing this Dharma being taught, will give rise to faith?
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, they are not sentient beings, yet they are not non-sentient beings."
"Born. Why is this? Subhūti, those who are called 'sentient beings' by the Tathāgata are not sentient beings; they are merely named 'sentient beings.

It exists; therefore, it is preserved. Since the names of what is taught are already profound, there is neither faith nor doubt. This so-called "teaching of no-teaching" does not depart from the *dharmakāya*;
being thus obscure and deep, one has no means to grasp it—what person could believe it? Therefore, he asks about it.
"He is neither a sentient being nor not a sentient being" means that he is not an ordinary sentient being (*pṛthagjana*), yet he is not someone who is not a sentient being of noble nature (*ārya*).
He stands out from the crowd and excels his peers; he is no ordinary person among ordinary people. Regarding the phrase "sentient beings, sentient beings," this reiterates the preceding text.
Regarding the phrase "The Tathāgata says they are not sentient beings, yet they are named 'sentient beings,'" this explains the preceding text.
It means that what are called ordinary sentient beings are in fact named "sentient beings of the noble nature. Thus Maitreya said: "What is spoken and the speaker are profound."
It is not that there are none capable of faith; it is neither sentient beings nor non-sentient beings; it is neither holy nor unholy. △ Nineteen:
Severing Doubts Regarding the Non-existence of Dharmas and How to Practice and Realize Them. Part One: The Question. Part Two: The Answer. First, the Question.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, when the Buddha attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is it that there is nothing to be attained?
This is the doubt manifested by Śūnyatā-prabhava. His intention refers to the previous third, twelfth, and thirteenth [sections].

All say that one does not attain bodhi. Since there is no dharma by which bodhi is attained, how is it that the Tathāgata cultivates and progresses through each stage, surpassing Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) and reaching Ultimate Wondrous Enlightenment (*anuttara-samyaksambodhi*), thereby realizing *anuttara-bodhi*? Therefore, he asks whether the Tathāgata’s attainment of bodhi is an "attainment of non-attainment.
Part Two: The Response (in two sections). First, clarifying bodhi; second, clarifying cultivation and realization.
First, the Bodhi is elucidated.
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Subhūti. Regarding this Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I [have realized it]."
Up to and including the point where not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended—this is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, Subhūti, this dharma is equal; it has no high or low. This is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha’s intention was this: if one wishes to know cultivation and realization, one must first recognize bodhi. Once bodhi is known, then cultivation and realization are known.
Regarding the statement that "not even the slightest dharma can be obtained," Maitreya said: "In that place there is not even the slightest dharma; thus one knows that bodhi is unsurpassed."
This refers to the locus where enlightenment (*bodhi*) is realized. It is simply called enlightenment when delusion is exhausted and awakening is fulfilled;
apart from this, what enlightenment could there be to be attained? This is why emptiness and quiescence are termed "enlightenment. This Dharma is equal—this is stated in its direct sense.
It is without high or low—this is stated in its reverse sense. As Maitreya said: "The Dharma-realm neither increases nor decreases; it is pure..."
The self-characteristic of equality means that it does not diminish among ordinary beings, and thus is not low; it does not increase among sages, and thus is not high.
The self-characteristic of purity is primordially thus. This refers to the single essence, which is called bodhi. The single essence is empty and quiescent;
such is the essence of bodhi. II. Explaining Cultivation and Realization.
By means of no-self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span, one cultivates all wholesome dharmas and thereby attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti, that which is called "wholesome dharmas" by the Tathāgata is indeed not wholesome dharmas;
it is merely designated as "wholesome dharmas."
Although the Dharma is empty and quiescent, it is choked by ignorance; although its essence is fundamentally equal, it is falsely divided into distinctions.
This does not mean that one can attain perfect enlightenment without cultivation; therefore, one cultivates through non-self and so forth.

"Non-self and so forth" refers to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), which is able to realize that afflictions are fundamentally empty and that the *dharmakāya* is fundamentally inherent; this is called the "cause of realization. It is like a lamp.

It is capable of destroying darkness and revealing objects. All wholesome dharmas—namely, the five perfections beginning with giving—are able to support *prajñā* (wisdom), severing afflictions and bringing about *bodhi* (enlightenment);

these are called "conditional causes" (*pratyaya-hetu*). Just as a lamp, though it destroys darkness and reveals objects, must necessarily rely upon oil and a wick as its supporting conditions, so too is it with these.
As for the statement that "that which is not a wholesome dharma is itself called a wholesome dharma," this refers to non-existence (*abhāva*).
The wholesome dharmas of humans and devas are subject to outflows (*āsrava*) and decline; these are the wholesome dharmas that are without outflows (*anāsrava*) and lead to the realization of Bodhi.
As Maitreya said: "Because there is the supreme skillful means and because it is free from the dharmas of outflows, that which is not a pure dharma is itself the pure dharma.
Thus, because they share the same essence of emptiness and quiescence, there is nothing to be attained; through the cultivation of non-self and so forth, one practices as one.
All wholesome dharmas are, moreover, identical in essence to emptiness and quiescence; therefore, there is nothing to be attained, yet it is attained.

Why, then, do you harbor doubts regarding cultivation and realization? Question: Previously, you stated that "non-existence" is called non-attainment, and subsequently that "equality" is called non-attainment.
Now, with the presence of cultivation and realization, the meanings appear contradictory. How can both be maintained? Answer: As for what is called "cultivation":
However, this merely eliminates the delusion that the dharmas of self are fundamentally non-existent, thereby revealing the reality that the virtues of self-nature are fundamentally present.
It is a cultivation without cultivation and a realization without realization; ultimately, not a single dharma can be attained.

How could there be cultivation, realization, or the attainment of even the slightest dharma? Therefore, this is in complete accord with what was stated previously. Question: The tenth doubt of the third [section].
Regarding the two instances of doubt, the thirteen doubts, and this present section, all state that one does not attain bodhi.

Are they not all equal in this regard? Answer: The third doubt concerns Kāśyapa attaining the fruit; the twelfth doubt concerns Sāradvatīputra establishing the cause; the thirteenth doubt concerns the non-existence of Buddha and Dharma;
whereas the present doubt concerns the existence of cultivation and realization. Although the phrasing is similar, the meaning is vastly different. Please examine this closely.
Spread it out so that there shall be no confusion.

Suppose there were a heap of the seven precious jewels, and someone were to take it and give it as a gift; yet if another person were to receive, uphold, read, recite,

nor one thousandth, nor ten millionth, nor one hundred billionth, nor even any part reachable by calculation, analogy, or comparison.

You do not realize that this sutra is most supreme, such that even the giving of jewels cannot equal it. This is truly because it is capable of...”
This is because one attains bodhi. Therefore, it is said: "Subhūti, as for the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system," and so forth.

This is because the sutra elucidates the ultimate truth, through which one awakens to understanding; based on this understanding, one gives rise to practice, and only then does one attain bodhi. If there were no gateway of teaching, [there would be no such attainment].
How could one know that this wondrous sūtra—which teaches that by means of the gateways of the Buddha’s teachings one exits the suffering of the triple world—is itself indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?

Yet even such [an indeterminate phenomenon] can still serve as a cause; how much more so this sūtra, which consists of the words and meanings manifested within the Buddha’s subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
These are exclusively untainted wholesome dharmas (*anāsrava-kuśala-dharma*) and not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). How could there be anyone who does not attain bodhi? Therefore, Maitreya said:
"Although it is called an indeterminate dharma, it is taught to be its cause; for this reason, a single jewel of the Dharma surpasses immeasurable worldly treasures.

It has no essence. Thus, they are vastly different.
△21. Severing Equality: How does one cross over sentient beings?
Subhūti, what do you think? You should not think that the Tathāgata has this thought: "I shall deliver sentient beings.
Subhūti, do not have such a thought. Why is that? In reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers.

It is lost in existence; therefore, it surpasses the previously acquired merit. As Maitreya said:
"Attaining superior patience and not losing it, one obtains the fruit of stainlessness and manifests the marks of superior merit. For this reason, a simile is taught:

The wondrous fruit is ultimately inexhaustible; what loss could there be? Furthermore, as for investigating why one who attains patience does not lose it:

"Not accepting" means that regarding the merit they perform, they are entirely without greedy attachment; this is called non-acceptance.
[One] receives [the fruit]. Now, if one creates merit while giving rise to greedy attachment, then since the cause is *sāsrava* (with outflows), the fruit will also be *sāsrava*.

One will merely evoke the thirty-two marks of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), but this is not called Buddhahood; when the retribution is exhausted, both cause and fruit are lost. This is truly as you have suspected.

The Buddha with the thirty-two marks is a manifestation of the nature of conformity; it appears through emptiness and purity, adorning the Dharma-body.
Why, then, do you doubt the loss of cause and fruit? Thus Maitreya says: "These merits have no retribution. This means there is no retribution that is *sāsrava* (with outflows);

The appearance of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions refers to the bodies of the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya*, which are the fruits of stainlessness.

Therein, only suchness (*tathatā*) and the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*) remain; from the beginning, they possess no material form or characteristics. Nevertheless, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, they appear spontaneously and naturally throughout the ten directions.

The intention is this: if one were to say that [the Buddha] was a transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), people would have no heart of reverence, and how could they be willing to believe and accept the Dharma he preached? Because he did not say so, all people revere him, and they all receive and uphold the teachings he proclaimed.
Thus, merit free from outflows (*anāsrava*) becomes naturally immeasurable. Indeed, it was precisely because he did not claim to be a transformation-body...
Thus, it can be known that transformation is entirely this Dharma. Furthermore, suchness is immovable and utterly devoid of discrimination;
this is what the ancients meant when they said, "It is precisely empty space that is capable of preaching.

If one uses a mind of birth and extinction to explain the Dharma of true reality, there will be nothing but delusion and nothing but defilement. How much more so when this is interspersed with fame and profit?
Is this not the mind [of those who preach]? Not only will there be no merit, but harm will surely follow. The retribution of Master Tan for the black gate is indeed something to be feared.
△ Twenty-seventh: Resolving the doubt regarding how to preach the Dharma upon entering quiescence.
Why is this? All conditioned phenomena are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow; they are like dew and also like lightning.
One should contemplate them in this way.
The Buddha’s intention is that although the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) preaches the Dharma, it is called the Tathāgata because it comes from nowhere.
If that were so, the Buddha would also be constantly in *nirvāṇa*. One might then doubt how *nirvāṇa* can be quiescent while the preaching of the Dharma is clamorous;
since movement and stillness are opposites, how can the Buddha constantly preach the Dharma without being obstructed by *nirvāṇa*?

Therefore, it is said that "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are equal," etc. The meaning is that the Buddha possesses the *pratyavekṣaṇājñāna* (wonderful observing wisdom), through which he contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena. As...

Although phenomena such as dreams and illusions appear to manifest with the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), they constantly abide in the principle of ultimate quiescence and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Engaging with existence, they do not dwell in existence; contemplating emptiness, they do not cling to emptiness. Thus, they are quiescent yet ever-active.
If one acts while remaining eternally quiescent, what further hindrance could there be? Furthermore, dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows are all metaphors for original emptiness;

like dew and lightning, they alike manifest swift extinction. To cause one to realize original emptiness is to not dwell upon any marks (*lakṣaṇa*); to enable one to know arising and ceasing is to exhort the practice of cultivation.
This perfectly accords with the school that shatters marks and skillfully demonstrates the contemplation of forgetting emotions. It is also...
One should not harbor doubts regarding this; it is merely an explanation of not grasping at marks and so forth.

By contemplating all conditioned phenomena as being like dreams and illusions, one personally neither grasps nor clings to them, thereby harmonizing with True Suchness (Tathatā) and remaining free from the movement of conceptual discrimination.
Nevertheless, because the sutras address the attachments of ordinary beings who grasp at things as being definitively real, they speak of them as being "like a dream" or "like an illusion.
However, speaking according to reality, conditioned phenomena *are* dreams; why then would one need to say they are "like a dream" or "like lightning"?
Therefore it is said: "What need is there to further perceive the affairs of this floating life? This very floating life is itself within a dream. Thus it is.
Thus, the three realms are a dream; the ten directions are a dream; delusion is certainly a dream, and awakening is also a dream.
From the three vehicles and the ten stages to bodhi and nirvana—wherein could one go that is not a dream? Only for one who dreams of dreaming can it not be called a "dream.
The speaker of the Dharma abides eternally prior to the arising of a single bubble, before even a single thought has occurred.
At the moment of sprouting, forms manifest through things; according to conditions, the Dharma is preached. It is naturally empty, numinous, and serenely illuminating—neither seeking nor grasping.
Since it does not grasp, it is as if one does not seek; it is like a dream, yet things themselves are the dream.
Now, if one gives rise to thoughts and conceives the notion, "I am like a dream," "I am like lightning," or "I am like a bubble or a shadow," then there is surely no way to overcome such [delusions].
Regarding these characteristics, one who cannot overcome their movement seeks the state of *tathatā* (suchness) which is immovable;
how is this any different from trying to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly? Therefore, know that one should contemplate in this way:
it is certainly not something that can be reached by a mind of conceptualization, discrimination, arising, and ceasing. Let the wise examine this in detail.
△ Third, the Section on Circulation:
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti, along with the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
and all the worldlings— devas, humans, and asuras— hearing what the Buddha had preached, were all greatly filled with joy.
Believing, accepting, and practicing accordingly.

Within this single fascicle of the sutra, both teacher and disciple are present; however, because the discourse is intended to highlight the supreme [teaching], it is attributed solely to the Buddha’s preaching.

As for the mention of Subhūti at the outset, it is because he is the primary recipient of the teaching (*ādhikārika*). Furthermore, while the fourfold assembly, as well as devas, humans, and asuras, are individually listed, [the bodhisattvas] are not mentioned...

Regarding the phrase "the spirits and deities, etc.": although not explicitly stated in the text, its meaning is implicitly contained within. They all rejoiced greatly, accepted it with faith, and practiced accordingly;
this was for the purpose of its widespread dissemination. As for their joy: they departed empty-handed but returned with substance.
Furthermore, because the one who preached is pure and the Dharma preached is pure, the fruit realized must also necessarily be pure; therefore, they rejoiced.
Furthermore, as for "faithful acceptance": not believing in any phenomena is faith in Prajñā; not grasping at any phenomena is acceptance of Prajñā.
This is called true understanding. To practice accordingly means that the mind arises without abiding, such as in giving while remaining detached from signs.

This is what is called true cultivation. Although the benefits received according to individual capacities may differ, once it has passed through the faculty of hearing, it forever becomes a seed for the Way.
The meaning of the sutra is inconceivable; how could its karmic fruition not also be inconceivable?
